1. No pre-merge reconciliation. worktree_merge merged without ever fetching origin/<target>, so once the remote had advanced the push could only be rejected. New `GitOperations::reconcile_target_with_origin` fetches first and classifies the result: AlreadyCurrent, FastForwarded, Diverged, FetchFailed, NoRemote. The handler calls it BEFORE the merge.
   - Strictly behind with no local-only commits: fast-forwarded automatically, with the receipt naming old tip -> new tip and the commit count (supervisor-directed: a fast-forward loses nothing and asking first would add a round trip to every merge).
   - Diverged: refused BEFORE any merge, naming both tips and both ahead/behind counts, with a fetch/merge/retry remedy and an explicit never-force-push line. Refusing after the merge would leave an unpublishable merge commit on the operator's local target to unpick.
   - Fetch failure (offline, auth, unreachable): never blocks. The merge proceeds against the local target and the receipt says so explicitly, warning the push may still be rejected.
   The ahead/behind comparison runs strictly AFTER the fetch, against freshly re-resolved refs; comparing beforehand would judge divergence against a stale tracking ref and could call a clean fast-forward a divergence, or miss a real one. How the fast-forward is applied depends on where the branch is checked out — `git merge --ff-only origin/<target>` in place, otherwise a compare-and-swap `update-ref` passing the old value so a concurrent move loses rather than clobbers — mirroring the existing merge venue split, because a bare update-ref against a checked-out branch would leave that working tree behind its own branch ref.

2. The rejection was classified as a generic failure and rendered with a hard-coded falsehood. `classify_push_rejection` collapsed every non-GH013 failure into one outcome, so the renderer could not distinguish "the remote moved" from "the network died", and the "is BEHIND" claim was baked into the format string rather than derived from the tips. It now has a `NonFastForward` arm matched on git's own stable markers, and the receipt names both tips, says origin is AHEAD, states plainly that a bare push cannot succeed until the two are reconciled, gives the fetch-and-merge remedy, and rules out force-pushing a shared target.

Nothing in this change force-pushes anything.

The pre-existing cas-5ee0/GH #137 fixture `publish_branch_to_origin_reports_not_pushed_on_diverged_remote` drove a real bare-remote non-fast-forward and asserted the generic NotPushed; it now asserts the precise NonFastForward and is renamed to match. task_title: GH #698: symbol index fails UTF-16 (BOM) source files with "stream did not contain valid UTF-8" forever — decode BOM-marked UTF-16/UTF-8-BOM files or skip them with a named reason instead of counting a permanent failure
close_reason:
GH #698 fixed; merged into the epic as 4f6ef15e (branch tip 11e573cc).

WHY THE WARNING COULD NEVER CLEAR: the indexer read every candidate with `fs::read_to_string` (cas-cli/src/daemon/indexing.rs), so a UTF-16 file failed with "stream did not contain valid UTF-8" and landed in the scan's error list. `failed_files` is derived as `eligible - indexed`, so that file stayed in the denominator permanently, and `cas index code` — the remediation the doctor line itself printed — re-read the same bytes and failed identically. The remedy was structurally incapable of working, which is why the reporter saw the same three files on Aug 31 and again on Sep 3.

WHAT IS NOW TRUE
- BOM-marked source files are decoded rather than failed: UTF-16 LE, UTF-16 BE, and UTF-8-with-BOM, in a new `daemon::source_text` module using std only. No new dependency was taken for three byte patterns.
- Decoding is strict, never lossy. An odd byte count after a UTF-16 BOM (truncated) and an unpaired surrogate (malformed) each produce a distinct named skip rather than U+FFFD replacement text indexed as if it were the author's code. Silent bad data in a symbol index outlives a loud error.
- A file that genuinely cannot be decoded is SKIPPED WITH A REASON and leaves the eligible denominator, so coverage reaches 100% of eligible instead of parking at 2,350/2,355. Skips are persisted separately from failed_files (migration 254, with the existing scan row preserved and defaulting to zero skips until the next scan reclassifies it), so a rerun cannot resurrect a warning no retry could clear.
- Doctor names the skipped files and attaches NO remediation to them, in both the warning and the healthy line. Printing "run `cas index code`" beside a file that can never be indexed is what trains operators to ignore doctor.

SECOND DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED, which the issue did not report and nobody had noticed: `read_to_string` ACCEPTED UTF-8-with-BOM, because a BOM is valid UTF-8. The BOM therefore reached the parser glued to the first token and the file indexed "successfully" with a subtly wrong first symbol. It produced bad data quietly instead of failing loudly, which is exactly why it went unreported. The BOM is now stripped, pinned by a test asserting the first symbol is findable by its real name.

task_title: Client half of revision-based conflict resolution (gated on petra-stella-cloud#41)
close_reason:
Client half of revision-based conflict resolution delivered; merged into the epic as 037a6300 (branch tip 642c1803).

WHAT IS NOW TRUE
- Server revisions decide sync conflicts; clocks decide only when revisions cannot. When both sides carry a revision and they differ, the higher wins and the timestamps are not consulted at all — that is what stops a machine with a wrong clock from silently winning or losing. Equal revisions, or either side missing one, fall through to the original timestamp comparison unchanged.
- Revision comparison arbitrates the KeepRecent strategy only. An explicit RemoteWins/LocalWins is an operator choice and stays authoritative (supervisor confirmed this is correct as shipped).
- `sync_revisions` ledger (migration 251) stores the last observed server revision per (entity_type, entity_id), monotonic on write so a replayed older envelope cannot roll a row backwards — that value becomes the base revision of the next push, and a rolled-back base would be rejected forever.
- Pull records each applied row's revision only AFTER the row is written, for entries, tasks, rules and skills, on both the personal and team paths. The ledger never claims a revision whose body this machine has not seen.
- Push declares the base revision as a decimal string when the ledger knows one and OMITS the key when it does not (omission selects the server's timestamp-LWW compatibility path). Any body-embedded revision is stripped first. Nothing is ever synthesized: the server drops a row whose revision it cannot parse, and a fabricated "0" against an existing row is a guaranteed conflict.
- Push receipts are consumed: the echoed new revision is read from the per-type accepted map (personal at top level, team nested under `synced`), so the next push declares an acceptable base without a re-pull. A revision_conflict is treated as retryable rather than parked — a lost race is a stale base, not a bad row — and the proven-stale base is FORGOTTEN rather than replaced with the server's current_revision, because adopting a revision whose body we never looked at would let the next push silently overwrite someone else's change.
- Conflict journal rows carry both revisions (migration 252, nullable), threaded through the single journal_local_overwrite funnel; strategy_label() distinguishes a "revision" decision from "timestamp_lww" so an audit can tell the two regimes apart.
- SyncQueue repairs its own sync_conflicts columns on init rather than depending on migration order: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cannot widen an existing table, so a store created before this change would otherwise fail every conflict insert until migration 252 happened to run. The queue owns those writes.

THE AUDIT THAT MADE IT REAL: wiring the resolver was not enough. upsert_task (the PERSONAL task pull) and upsert_skill compared updated_at INLINE and never called resolve_conflict, so the comparison was unit-tested and would almost never have run against a real sync. Both now go through remote_supersedes_local. Because the revision arrives on the raw wire row while the decision happens inside typed upsert helpers, the pull stages incoming revisions on the syncer (cleared at pull start) instead of threading an argument through six signatures where one missed site would silently revert that entity kind to clock comparison.

CONTRACT VERIFIED LIVE AND READ-ONLY, BEFORE CODING AND AGAIN BEFORE CLAIMING RULES/SKILLS: revision is present on 100% of pulled rows (personal tasks 114/114, entries 1019/1019, dependencies 3533/3533; team 111/111, 79/79, 4401/4401) and is a decimal STRING — a lexicographic compare ranks "9" above "10" and would invert every conflict from a row's tenth edit onward, which a dedicated test pins. Rules and skills genuinely carry revisions too (personal rules 2/2; team rules 22/22, skills 3/3), so recording them is contract-backed rather than synthesized. Push-side contract read from the deployed cloud source: the field is plain revision per entity object, omission selects legacy, a malformed value drops the row as invalid_revision, and reason is treated as an open string.

TESTS (scoped filtersets — a plain substring filter runs zero tests under the guard): test(/^cloud::/) 325 passed, test(/^cli::cloud::/) 81 passed, test(/^migration::/) 150 passed; combined filterset 556. Supervisor's gate on this tip: 1148 lib tests across cloud::, cli::cloud::, migration::, store::, cli::doctor::, mcp::tools::core::task plus mcp_tools_test and cli_test integration, all passed. The acceptance evidence is a real pull, not the unit API: a full team pull where the cloud row is an hour newer by the clock but one revision behind, and the local row survives; it failed before commit 642c1803. Clock skew is covered in both directions, plus a backward-compatibility matrix over all three revision-absence combinations against newer-remote, newer-local and identical timestamps.

Commits: caf73435 (comparison, ledger, journal), 315efac8 (base revision on push, receipts, revision_conflict), 9c9090d9 (epic merge, m250 collision renumber to m251/m252, migration::tests cursor pin and its three pending vectors moved to 252), 642c1803 (make the comparison fire on real pulls).

OPERATOR NOTE FOR THE RELEASE: the default team strategy is RemoteWins, so on a default-configured team pull the revision comparison does not fire — RemoteWins already answers the question. Revisions arbitrate KeepRecent: personal pulls, and teams configured for "keep whichever is newer".

task_title: verification add fails fast with "database is locked" under store contention while coordination message writes in the same seconds succeed — add busy_timeout/retry parity across write paths
close_reason:
Root cause: not a missing busy_timeout. The verification add handler already set the 5s SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT (verification_tools.rs:466); the defect was conn.unchecked_transaction() at :473, which is DEFERRED. The block reads the dispatch and the verifier capability before it inserts, so it held a read snapshot and had to UPGRADE to a writer — and SQLite answers that upgrade with SQLITE_BUSY without ever invoking the busy handler, because blocking there could deadlock two readers upgrading at once. The configured timeout was therefore silently irrelevant and the call failed in milliseconds, which is exactly why four consecutive verification writes failed while single-statement message and notes writes in the same seconds succeeded: their busy handler does apply.

Reproduced twice before any fix. Outside CAS with sqlite3 at .timeout 5000: BEGIN; SELECT; (foreign commit); INSERT fails immediately, while BEGIN IMMEDIATE; SELECT; INSERT succeeds. In-code as a permanent regression test: a_deferred_read_then_write_fails_instantly_despite_the_busy_timeout asserts the failure arrives in under 500ms with a 5s timeout configured.

Delivered:
1. shared_db::begin_immediate_with_retry acquires BEGIN IMMEDIATE — where the busy handler applies — with the same jittered backoff as with_write_retry. The retry envelope is strictly narrower than the transactional block: retries occur only while acquiring the lock, and once the transaction is open the body runs exactly once, so the single-use verifier capability the body consumes cannot be double-consumed. The verification add handler uses it.
2. cas-cli/src/memory_migration/reindex.rs read every knowledge page body from disk inside its write transaction, holding the store's write lock across N filesystem reads. Bodies are now read first; the transaction contains only database work.
3. Sibling audit: three sites inspected and deliberately left unchanged because each writes first and therefore takes the lock where the busy handler applies — purge_fixtures.rs:233, recording_store/store_impl.rs:512, event_store.rs:321.
4. journal_size_limit = 64 MiB on connection open, pinned by a test, so a long-lived writer fleet stops leaving a 389 MB WAL behind for 1,137 live frames. TRUNCATE-on-quiet was deliberately excluded per supervisor ruling: a checkpoint policy can stall a writer and belongs in its own task.
5. The give-up error states the wait attempted — "database busy for 5.3s across 6 attempt(s); another connection held the write lock for the whole wait" — instead of the bare sqlite text that made the original report un-triageable.

Verification ver-6b6863f4a622 pass on vdispatch-5cea53cc256cca145d7a4fd7971b2a4f.

task_title: cas update -y runs the all-projects refresh with the PRE-update binary, so fixes in the version being installed do not apply in the same run — a second `cas update` is needed (observed installing 3.15.2: refresh still showed 16 projects and the gabber-studio ledger wedge)

`cas update` now runs its post-install phases with the binary it just installed, so a single update converges. Delivered on factory/nimble-hound-64 (07f7a242 red tests, fcad7850 fix, 75b200f3 single-receipt contract, d3588a20 supervisor rulings); merged into epic cas-cfd3, epic tip 9b992820 after the supervisor resolved a CHANGELOG union against v3.15.3's main. Cause, confirmed in source: execute() called refresh_all_projects in the same process that had just swapped its own binary — the pre-update image — so schema migrations, the all-projects refresh, the user-level store and skills sync all ran the old version's code. Installing 3.15.2 from 3.15.1 refreshed 16 projects instead of 43, omitted user_level_store, and still reported the gabber-studio ledger wedge that 3.15.2 fixes. - perform_update delegates the post-install phases to the newly installed binary through that same --post-swap child and returns a BinaryUpdateOutcome carrying the child's receipt; execute() no longer re-runs the refresh in the old image.

- Every refresh receipt carries refresh_binary_version, the version of the process that actually did the work, and --json emits one combined document instead of two.
- The parent verifies the child's reported version equals the version just installed and fails loudly on any mismatch, including a child that reports nothing — the guard against a stale `cas` answering instead of the installed binary. Keeping is not a change, so a run over an override stays idempotent.
- `report.allowlist` is now the effective policy, so drift is measured against what will actually dispatch, and "already-configured" cannot be printed while a shadowing file drifts.
- A project file that names no hub route is left untouched and reported with the exact routes to add, rather than offered a re-run that cannot work.

task_title: Foreign-row peer scan treats every known_repos row as a project and WARNs on test scratch roots ("fresh-proxy … no such table: tasks"); registry must skip artifacts/scratch roots and `cas known-repos` needs a `forget <path>` verb
close_reason:
Merged into epic/epic-cas-doctor-warnings-the-operator-cannot-clear-cas-8094 as df0e8550 (factory/agile-crane-5 @ aa384a61; 2f11e28e tests-first, aa384a61 implementation). (1) Registry writes skip disposable roots. `store/known_repos.rs` gains `RegistrySkip{Artifacts,Scratch,Temp}` + `registry_skip()`; `register_repo`, `register_repo_strict` and `worktree::discovery::seed` all consult it and log the reason at debug. A skip returns Ok, not Err, so the boot paths that `?` the strict call keep booting. Artifacts roots resolve from three sources — the default host artifacts directory, the candidate's own `.cas/config.toml` (an artifacts copy carries the config it was copied from), and the ambient project store — so a configured `[factory] artifacts_root` is honoured. The temp rule is narrow on purpose: only a directory directly under the system temp directory carrying a `temp_hygiene::TEMP_ROOT_PREFIXES` name. A blanket system-temp rule was tried and rejected, because every TestEnvGuard fixture HOME is itself a system-temp directory; that rule would have silently disabled registration across the suite and for any operator whose checkout lives on a temp mount.

(2) Peer enumeration separates "not a project store" from "unreadable". `read_snapshot` split into `open_read_only` + `snapshot_from_conn`; new `read_peer_snapshot` returns `Ok(None)` when the peer DB has no `tasks` table. New `SkippedPeer` / `ForeignRowReport::peers_skipped` / `NOT_A_PROJECT_STORE`; `summary()` wraps `comparison_summary()` so the skipped clause appears on every branch, including the zero-peer branch where a host whose only other row is a scratch copy would otherwise read "0 project DB(s) compared" with no explanation. `peers_skipped` is deliberately absent from the doctor status expression (doctor.rs:1663) so it can never drive WARN. Genuine read failures stay loud in `peers_unreadable`, and the local DB still fails hard if it has no `tasks` table.

task_title: Flaky under load: hub_clean_home_test::concurrent_start_and_restart_leave_exactly_one_lock_owner failed once in the v3.15.1 release gate's full nextest run, passes 3/3 in isolation
close_reason:
Delivered on factory/true-panther-6, frozen at a544276a96e28a952f08b1d2f0acb9389ccd8000; merged by the supervisor into epic cas-cfd3, tip 420ee07d. Verified ver-3bb02e67a9d9 (pass) on vdispatch-ba3604c3c4f6433f0b13b021d2b685d4.

Durable evidence: /home/pippenz/.cas/artifacts/cas-bf90/ (README.md, after-24-iterations.txt, and the four harness scripts). Reproduction command: /home/pippenz/.cas/artifacts/cas-bf90/measure.sh 24 8 — runs `hub start --port 0 --tailscale-serve` and `hub restart --port 0 --tailscale-serve` concurrently against one private HOME under 8 CPU spinners, tallying failures per command, both-fail, and lock-wait timeouts. The recorded receipt was produced by that durable copy.

ROOT CAUSE. Not a timeout being too small. Concurrent `hub start` and `hub restart` both stop the old hub and both try to launch a replacement; whichever arrives second waits on the machine lock, which the winner's brand-new healthy hub legitimately holds for its whole life. Every waiter asked "is the lock FREE?" when the caller cares about "is a satisfying hub LIVE?" — an unsatisfiable condition, not a slow one, which is why no budget increase could have fixed it.

FIX. RelaunchIntent makes the caller's purpose explicit on the shared stop path. stop_with_output takes Option<RelaunchIntent>: Some(..) lets the wait resolve on observing a live hub satisfying those flags; None (plain `hub stop`) is byte-for-byte unchanged, because for stop a live hub is the opposite of success. StopOutcome::AlreadySatisfied forces callers to return rather than fall through — load-bearing twice: the teardown after the wait (remove_process_record, cgroup kill, Tailscale disable) would otherwise dismantle a healthy hub the command does not own, and falling through would recurse stop -> start -> Restart -> stop forever, since with `--port 0` decide_live_start always chooses Restart. The wait never accepts the hub being replaced as its own replacement. Wired into all three stop-to-relaunch callers: the `hub restart` arm, the flags-differ branch of `hub start`, and restart_stale_hub for `cas update`. The launch waiter got the same treatment via running_hub_satisfies_request + wait_for_lock_or_satisfying_hub.

BEFORE / AFTER, same harness, concurrent start+restart under load:
- Before: the losing command failed in ~80% of iterations, ALWAYS after burning the full 10s HUB_LIFECYCLE_TIMEOUT.
- After: 24 iterations, any_fail=0, start_fail=0, restart_fail=0, both_fail=0, lock_wait_timeouts=0; every iteration 150-320ms.
- The integration test itself: failing at 10.18s -> passing at 1.426s.

PER-SITE ATTRIBUTION. Mid-fix, with only the launch waiter done, every residual failure was attributable by message provenance: 5x wait_for_process_and_lock_release, 5x the record-absent bare wait_for_instance_lock, 0x the new launch waiter. Giving the new waiter distinct wording is what made that measurable; three sites previously emitted identical text.

WHERE THE LAST BUG HID. After wiring intent into the `start` flags-differ branch and restart_stale_hub, the test still failed: the `hub restart` arm was `stop(cli)?` + `start(...)`, so it went through the plain stop wrapper and carried no intent. The strengthened assertion caught that deterministically on the first run. The old assertion was `any(success)`, which passed whenever either command happened to win and so hid a ~80% loser-failure rate entirely; without changing it this fix would have shipped looking correct.

SCOPE. serve_foreground's fail-fast acquire_instance_lock unchanged; terminate_failed_launch untouched; no timeout constant changed. wait_for_process_and_lock_release removed as dead code, its quiescence rule and exact error text preserved in wait_for_stop_or_satisfying_hub.

TESTS. hub_clean_home_test 8/8 (was 7/8 with the concurrent test red), lib hub:: 129, lib cli::hub 33, lib cli::update 31. Six new unit tests on running_hub_satisfies_request, and a new integration test proving plain `hub stop` still fails and names why while a hub holds the lock past the deadline. Supervisor's independent gate on the delivered tip: hub::/cli::hub lib 94, hub_clean_home_test 8/8, and 8/8 again on the merged tree.

BOTH-FAIL, stated plainly rather than papered over: the originally reported both-commands-failed assertion was NEVER reproduced, across 148 runs (48 full-test executions = 240 concurrent pairs, plus 100 micro-iterations) at loads up to 98, above the 25-51 of the original gate failure. The supervisor-authorised scratch-build diagnostic (HUB_LAUNCH_TIMEOUT 5s -> 200ms, reverted) established it is not reachable via the readiness path: the hub still published a live record in time and the roles merely flipped. The fix does not depend on that interleaving — it removes an unsatisfiable wait for every waiter, so the unreproduced case is covered by construction rather than by guesswork.

TWO OF MY OWN DIAGNOSES WERE WRONG and are recorded as wrong in the task notes: (1) "the launcher's own child holds the lock and starves the peer" — false, the launcher execs the hub in the same pid and terminate_failed_launch kills it; (2) "HUB_LAUNCH_TIMEOUT being tighter than HUB_LIFECYCLE_TIMEOUT is the trigger" — false, disproved by the diagnostic. Both were corrected to the supervisor before any code was written on them.

Release note, Fixed: concurrent `cas hub start` / `cas hub restart` no longer stall ten seconds and report a spurious failure when another command has already brought up the hub you asked for.

WHAT LANDED

QueueOrigin {RegisteredAgent{agent_id}, Daemon, Unattributed}; the agent id is the registry id, not a display name, so role resolution cannot be spoofed by naming someone. task_title: Canonical worker merge leaves another linked epic checkout stale
close_reason:
A canonical worker merge no longer strands another linked checkout of the target branch.

ROOT CAUSE, reproduced before implementing and corrected from my own earlier lead: not branch_is_checked_out_here, but GitOperations::merge_branch_via_temp_worktree (cas-cli/src/worktree/git.rs). It merges in an ephemeral detached worktree and advances the branch with compare_and_swap_ref, i.e. update-ref. Git refuses `checkout` of one branch in two worktrees, but update-ref bypasses that protection and notifies nobody, so a second linked worktree keeps its old index and working tree while the ref moves. A fixture builds that exact shape in a temporary repository and, before the fix, failed with `D  delivered.txt` — the sibling reporting the merged content as a staged deletion, the same phantom reverse diff the epic integration checkout showed.

DELIVERED BEHAVIOUR, every branch decided before anything is written:
- The inventory of checkouts holding the target is read repo-wide from `git worktree list --porcelain`. If git cannot answer, the merge refuses with CheckoutInventoryUnavailable before the temp worktree, the merge and the compare-and-swap — an unknown inventory never authorizes an advance.
- A holder with uncommitted work refuses with TargetCheckedOutDirty before any ref change, naming the path, the change count and the tip the target is still at. Untracked files count, because an untracked file exists nowhere else. The guidance is commit or stash with an explicit "do NOT reset or check it out over"; tests assert no reset or read-tree recipe can appear in that text.
- A holder that is still clean is advanced by git's two-tree `read-tree -m -u <old_tip> <new_tip>`, which refuses when an entry is not up to date, so the decision is git's at the moment it writes rather than ours from an earlier check. Identity is re-verified at write time, so a checkout switched to another branch or detached is left alone with the branch it moved to named.
- Any refusal to refresh reaches the operator: notes are recorded and drained by append_stale_checkout_notes into the same receipt that carries the reconcile line, stating the ref advance, that the refresh declined, git's reason, and that nothing was overwritten — and deliberately not claiming what that checkout now contains, which is unknowable. A poisoned notes mutex recovers its contents instead of dropping safety warnings.
- The merge still succeeds rather than becoming a retryable failure after a committed merge.

GH #73 CANNOT REGRESS, verified through the venue split rather than assumed: a shared checkout on the target takes MergeVenue::SharedCheckout and merges in place, and one on any other branch never holds the target, so the new refusal is unreachable there. merging_still_leaves_the_primary_checkout_untouched_when_no_sibling_holds_the_target asserts unrelated residue still merges, the primary branch does not move, and the merged file is not checked out into it.

EVIDENCE (rule-173, real counts): scripts/run-scoped-tests.sh -p cas --lib worktree::git reported 75 tests run, 75 passed, 5315 skipped; scripts/run-scoped-tests.sh -p cas --lib workflow::worktree_ops reported 32 tests run, 32 passed, 5358 skipped; cargo check -p cas --lib --tests exited 0 with no new warnings. Coverage includes the reproduction, the clean refresh, the dirty refusal, an unstaged edit injected into the refresh window, a staged edit injected into the same window (content byte-identical and still staged), a checkout switched to another branch, an unreadable inventory proving ref/HEAD/status/files all unmutated, and the receipt-assembly seam with one-shot draining. Negative proof: disabling only the refresh step reproduces `D  delivered.txt`; the file was restored from a copy under artifacts rather than git checkout and the suite re-run green. The supervisor independently ran the combined git and caller suites (exit 0, 75/32) and exact-tip CI 33940661343 SUCCEEDED.

Limitations are recorded on this task as a decision note and are not overstated here: this is a guarded git transition, not a lock; the branch-identity re-check is itself time-of-check; coverage is single-machine local git; the receipt test pins the assembly seam rather than an end-to-end MCP response; and nothing here repairs an already stranded checkout, which the supervisor refreshed independently and I never touched.

task_title: Resolve assembled release retrieval precision regression without weakening oracle
close_reason:
The assembled 3.17.0 candidate meets the committed retrieval baseline again, by an explained correction rather than a lowered bar. The oracle is untouched: baseline.json and REGRESSION_TOLERANCE were never edited and the rebaseline path was never run.

REPRODUCED FIRST, exactly as reported: retrieval_eval_test.rs:1011, ambient_packet live_tiers and all_working, precision@5 0.0714 -> 0.0565, 20.8% relative against a 10% tolerance.

ROOT CAUSE, established with row-level evidence rather than inference. A detached scratch worktree at the pre-change commit 600288d1 ran the identical diagnostic over a byte-identical fixture, so code was the only variable, and it reproduced the committed baseline exactly (P@5 0.071429, 8 hitting cases, mean_returned 1.428571, 24 silent). Against that, the entire -0.8334 precision mass delta was three cases: n01 0.500 -> 0.000, c12 and n02 0.500 -> 0.333. The lost hit was n01, whose task is cas-096e: its packet went from ['2026-08-07-8','2026-08-06-13'] to EMPTY, dropping a memory tagged cas-096e whose body opens "CI wall-clock work on cas-src (cas-096e/GH #142 ...)" — that case's own prior learnings, correctly labelled relevant. So this was a product regression, not a stale oracle. Mechanism: cas-fa938 rightly stopped structural identity terms manufacturing relevance, but `task=` was filtered out of query terms while `binding` only tested query.task_id == row.id, which is true for the task row itself and never for a memory ABOUT that task. Such a row was neither a lexical term nor structurally bound, so it was unreachable. An early expiry hypothesis was disproved and withdrawn: the fixture carries no valid_until and the materialiser never sets one, so the staleness comparison cannot move it, and entries are seeded as created = now - age_days - position, so wall-clock drift shifts all ages together and is not a confound.

CORRECTION, two narrow parts because the first alone measured as inert. names_current_task lets an exact, token-bounded occurrence of the CURRENT task id contribute binding only; and the retriever additionally reads rows naming that id, since binding could not rescue a row the SQL prefilter never fetched. Identity buys retrieval and binding, never a lexical score: scoring terms are unchanged, and staleness, expiry, privacy and eligibility all still apply. Supplemental rows are filtered by the same exact binding rule before the union, so a substring SQL match cannot introduce unbound noise; deduplication is keyed on (surface, id) because ids are unique only within their own table; and the token scan uses match_indices, so a multi-byte task id or body cannot panic on a character boundary.

RESULT, same fixture and diagnostic across all three trees: precision@5 0.071429 baseline -> 0.056548 broken -> 0.090774 fixed, recall@5 0.033801 -> 0.030825 -> 0.050765, cases with a hit 8 -> 7 -> 11, silent 24 -> 20 -> 17. The fixed tree is 27.1% ABOVE the committed baseline, n01 recovers its labelled-relevant row, and 18 cases now differ from the baseline ranking, so the improvement is broad rather than a single-case patch.

task_title: Skill frontmatter can emit invalid YAML: duplicated escape_yaml leaves backslashes raw in both live writers
close_reason:
Generated frontmatter is now produced by one proven serializer and read back by a parser, so a description like `Use C:\project: inspect` no longer emits YAML that a reader rejects with `found unknown escape character 'p'`.

ROOT CAUSE: three hand-rolled `escape_yaml` copies — cas-cli/src/sync/skills.rs, crates/cas-core/src/sync/skills.rs and crates/cas-core/src/sync/specs.rs — had already drifted, the spec copy escaping backslashes while the skill copies left them raw inside a quoted scalar.

SHARED SEAM: crates/cas-core/src/sync/yaml_scalar.rs exposes cas_core::sync::yaml_scalar and serves all three writers, each keeping its local escape_yaml as a one-line delegate so call sites and harness-specific metadata policy are untouched. Neither SkillSyncer is deleted. serde_yaml 0.9 was added to cas-core; it was already in the tree via cas-cli, so Cargo.lock gains a single edge rather than a package. Every escaping path is a real serializer: serde_yaml emits whenever it can do so on one line, and serde_json — already a cas-core dependency — produces the single-line form otherwise, because a JSON string literal is a valid YAML double-quoted scalar. That claim is proven against a YAML parser over the whole corpus, not asserted. Serializing a &str cannot fail, so the invariant is stated with expect rather than swallowed into an empty scalar that would blank a description.

READER: extract_yaml_value parses the frontmatter and looks the key up exactly, preserving the typed-field behaviour callers depend on — a YAML boolean reads back as "true"/"false" text because user-invocable and disable-model-invocation are compared as those strings, while a sequence, mapping or null reads as absent. Legacy recovery runs only when the parser rejects the document AND matches an unindented line whose key is followed immediately by ':', so an unrelated malformed document cannot answer `description` from `description_extra` and an indented key nested under `hooks:` is not lifted out.

task_title: Beth Barbeau logged out every ~10 minutes WHILE actively working on a video from the text flow
close_reason:
Merged and verified: c7b50f90a is an ancestor of origin/epic/epic-customer-debt-burn-down-2026-08-14-every-outs-cas-ae08 via merge dfe1b01fb (checked with git merge-base --is-ancestor after a fetch, not assumed from the supervisor note).

ROOT CAUSE. Two structural defects in AUTOMATIC session teardown — neither is a timer, and there is no ten-minute anything in the product.

D1: clearAllSessions() called the backend logout with no argument. The backend revokes unless told literally {revoke:false}, and revokeUserSessions(uid) kills every refresh token the account holds on every device and invalidates the 14-day session cookie (verified checkRevoked=true). Every caller of clearAllSessions is automatic — the hourly revalidation tick, the visibility handler, the page-load stale-session plugin, and initializeAuth's already-initialized recovery branch reached from every route guard. So one transient blip — Firebase losing its IndexedDB connection in an iOS webview, which this repo already documents at auth-persistence.ts:78-82 — permanently destroyed the silent re-mint that exists to keep a user signed in. It was self-sustaining: after a revoke the next forced refresh throws auth/user-token-expired, which is in REVOCATION_CODES, which calls clearAllSessions, which revokes again. The backend's own comment already warns of exactly this loop; handleTokenExpiry was given {revoke:false} for that reason and clearAllSessions never was. Revocation is now opt-in — a global irreversible action should not be what you get when nobody thought about it — and the one caller that means "log out everywhere", the sign-out button, states it. Side effect worth knowing: exiting impersonation no longer revokes the impersonated CUSTOMER's tokens on all their devices.

D2: the public SMS audit page /audit/<postId>?s=<token> — the customer's exact entry path — was guarded only inside handleTokenExpiry, whose comment calls itself "the single chokepoint every caller funnels through". It is not. clearAllSessions redirected to /sign-in from anywhere outside an exact-match allowlist that /audit was never on, so recoverStaleSession and the stale-session plugin could throw a customer working from a texted link out to the sign-in screen. Both paths now share one predicate, prefix-guarded so /audits (the signed-in list page, which should redirect) is not swallowed.

PROD EVIDENCE (PostHog project 462584, prod; staging 462585 explicitly excluded). The forced-logout throw in getIdToken went 2 / 22 / 686 / 770 per day across 08-10..08-13, against total $exception volume of 7 / 23 / 714 / 837 the same days — the throw is essentially the entire spike, and the control proves the query binds. 76% of those events (1,332/1,746) are iOS/WebKit. About 50 user-hours show three or more sign-ins in one hour alongside heavy /audit activity: users bounced while working, not users failing to log in. Measured gaps between consecutive user_signed_in events ran from seconds to 129 minutes, including one at 10m57s — bursty and irregular, which is what "seemed like every 10 min or so" actually describes.

task_title: Same reel re-submitted after a successful audit mints a new post and a new charge — URL dedupe only covers in-flight/15min
close_reason:
Merged to the epic branch at 1363a6c6b (b84a09de is now contained in origin/epic/epic-customer-debt-burn-down-2026-08-14-every-outs-cas-ae08 — verified).

Completed-audit URL dedupe. Prevalence measured on prod BEFORE proposing a policy, which inverted the task's premise: the "edited re-cut" case the task told us to protect does not exist, because Instagram/TikTok/YouTube never let you replace the video behind an existing URL — a re-cut publishes to a NEW URL and can never match this dedupe. Only 10 of 472 dupes were direct uploads at all. What is real: 247 re-submits of an already-audited URL in 180 days, 235 charged, 4,710 credits burned across 173 workspaces; 68% of that waste landed within 15 MINUTES of the audit that had just finished, and the single biggest pattern (70 cases) was texting a reel in and pasting the same link into the web app minutes later — one intent, two charges. The genuine reason to re-audit a stable URL is refreshed engagement numbers, which argues for a bounded window rather than leaving terminal posts open.

Fix: same workspace + same normalized URL + a finished audit inside the window returns that audit and charges nothing. The dedupe hit short-circuits before debitPostAudit, so "free" is structural rather than a special case in the billing path. Outside the window, or with explicit forceReaudit intent, a fresh charged audit runs. Failed runs stay re-submittable throughout, so a retry after a failure always starts a fresh run. Window = POC_COMPLETED_AUDIT_DEDUPE_WINDOW_HOURS, default 24h (recovers 84% of the waste), 0 disables; a malformed value falls back to the default rather than to 0, so a typo cannot silently re-open the double-charge.

Collateral fixed in the same change, without which this would be a billing rule rather than a finished feature: daily-audit no longer records a deduped pre-existing post as today's run (it would have found an instantly-complete audit and re-texted a report the customer already got); SMS senders receive the audit they already have instead of the "analyzing…" ack followed by permanent silence (no pipeline runs on this path, so no completion SMS would ever fire); universal-input stops claiming it is analyzing when it just handed back an existing report, and states the repeat was not charged.

Verification: 17 new tests, 13 demonstrated FAILING against pre-fix source via git stash (the 2 that pass pre-fix are guards asserting current behaviour is preserved — forceReaudit and window=0). tsc clean; 1,425 tests green across poc/items/sms/daily-audit; no new lint errors introduced.

Carried forward, not absorbed here: the 24h default is on Daniel's queue for ratification with the env-var escape hatch; and there is no UI affordance for forceReaudit yet, so a user who genuinely wants an in-window re-audit has no button — recorded by the supervisor for filing to an Opus worker per the standing UI preference.

task_title: web-fallback endpoint: require proof-of-phone-control (public unauth route grants free audits + enables phone-spoofing)
close_reason:
Free-audit mint budget on per-IP + global daily axes (non-fabricable), charged only on actual mint, all fail-closed; 8 red pre-change tests; jest 802 + bootstrap-smoke green. AC3 met; AC1/AC2 void per ruling; spoofed-phone half → cas-d690.

DETAIL FOR THE RECORD.

The defect: poc.service.ts:315 grants any workspace with owner===null && !hasReceivedFreeAudit one free PAID audit for its lifetime, and sms-responder.service.ts:879 skips the affordability pre-check on the same condition. The public @Public() web-fallback route mints exactly such a workspace for any phone string it has not seen, so the real economic bound was ONE FREE PAID AUDIT PER DISTINCT PHONE STRING — an identity the attacker mints for free by inventing an E.164 string. The pre-existing per-phone limit therefore capped an axis the attacker owns: a speed limit, not a cap. The window counters bounded the rate and never the total.

The fix: a mint budget on per-IP-per-day (WEB_FALLBACK_MINT_IP_DAILY_MAX, default 3) and GLOBAL-per-day (WEB_FALLBACK_MINT_GLOBAL_DAILY_MAX, default 200). Charged ONLY when the submission would actually mint — the phone has neither an existing workspace nor an existing account, mirroring the two skip conditions in ensureWorkspaceForPhoneUnowned. Every other property follows from that exemption: a returning submitter is never charged, so exhausting the global budget pauses NEW mints and cannot lock out anyone already in the funnel; the per-IP cap is checked FIRST and short-circuits WITHOUT touching the global counter, so one capped IP cannot drain the day's budget and take the non-US funnel down with it; a malformed phone is not charged, so garbage is not a cheap way to exhaust the cap. Both counters and the eligibility lookup FAIL CLOSED (503). Enforced in the GUARD, before the handler, so a refused submission leaves no CRM lead, no sms_messages row, no workspace. It runs after the window limits deliberately — it costs up to two indexed DB reads and an unauthenticated caller must not be able to aim those at the database at will. A global-cap bind logs at ERROR; legitimate volume is ~19 new phones/day (562 submissions / 552 distinct phones over 30d), so 200/day is ~10x headroom and a bind means attack or growth.

REUSE, NOT A SECOND MECHANISM (the supervisor's reconciliation instruction): this adds NO new proof-of-identity primitive and does not touch cas-57f1's claim path. cas-57f1's server-issued signed claim token remains the possession proof; cas-0070 adds only the mint-path cost cap, which cas-57f1's own note assigned here ("Minting is separately capped by cas-0070"). No OTP, no country-dependent SMS wall, so Daniel's cas-e8c6 ruling is untouched and no international friction is reintroduced.

Deliberately NOT touched: debitPostAudit's per-workspace lifetime grant also serves the real inbound-SMS funnel; narrowing it there would change behaviour for users this task is not about.

EVIDENCE, no proxy checks. New src/sms/web-fallback-rate-limit.guard.spec.ts (the guard had NO unit spec before). Against the PRE-change guard: 8 failed, 6 passed, 14 total. The 8 red are the evidence — per-IP cap, global-not-charged-after-IP-refusal, global cap, under-both-caps charges both axes, day bucketing, fail-closed on lookup, fail-closed on counter, non-positive-cap config rejection. Stated rather than counted: the 3 exemption/malformed cases passed pre-change VACUOUSLY (no mint keys existed to touch) and the 3 window cases are regression pins. Post-change 14/14. Per-worktree deps (pnpm install --frozen-lockfile exit 0, npx prisma generate exit 0, no symlinks to the main checkout): tsc --noEmit clean; jest src/sms src/workspaces --runInBand → 59 suites / 802 tests; full unit suite 290/291 suites and 4071/4072 tests, the single failure (conversion-sms-enroll "sets absolute expectedAt from enroll") PROVEN pre-existing by stashing the whole diff and re-running at the base — identical failure, wall-clock-shaped assertion in a file this diff does not touch; nest build + scripts/bootstrap-smoke-test.js exit 0, "dependencies resolved (59 modules)", which is what proves the new PrismaService injection into a guard is wired since hand-constructed unit guards would not catch bad DI; eslint 0 errors on all touched files.

close_reason:
SPIKE complete. All 5 questions answered with measurements against deployed staging + the Neon staging branch; no product code changed (working tree clean, throwaway specs live only in the artifacts dir).

DOMINANT CAUSE, named with numbers: GET /api/v1/workspaces/all returns 33,081 rows x 36 fields = 29,598,889 bytes (1,336,389 gzipped), unpaginated and uncached (workspace.service.ts:518 — findMany with `include:` and no select/take/where deletedAt). pages/dashboard/index.vue:2115 fires it unconditionally on mount as the FIRST of five serial awaits, solely to populate one dropdown. Feeding that array into a `persist: true` Pinia store (stores/workspace.ts:1230, no pick/omit) blocks the main thread for 4,146-4,728 ms in a SINGLE long task.

Q1 waterfall: /workspaces/all = 1,749 ms wall / 1,328 ms TTFB — 4x the next-slowest request and the only one over a second. Full 16-row table in findings.md.
Q2 server vs client: NEITHER is the DB — EXPLAIN ANALYZE of the equivalent SQL is 45.132 ms, all shared-buffer hits, no missing index. ~1.7 s TTFB is Prisma hydration + JSON.stringify in Node. The client is worse: 4.5 s. CPU-profile ancestry attributes it to (a) 688 ms `serialize` <- `cg` <- `$subscribe.detached` = pinia-plugin-persistedstate, and (b) 661+105 ms Vue deep-watch traverse()/ownKeys Proxy traps. JSON.parse of the 29.6 MB body is only 50 ms, so parsing is NOT the cost.
Q3 "freezes" = one unbroken 4.1-4.7 s main-thread task, measured 4 times. Not a stuck request (all 200) and not table rendering — QSelect virtual-scrolls (30 DOM nodes for 33,081 options; 131 ms to open). Row counts: workspaces 33,081 / projects 33,076 / items 402 / accounts 86.
Q4 yes — it fetches metadata for EVERY workspace before any is selected, but only to fill the chooser; items stay scoped to one workspace. Not necessary: 3 of 36 fields are used, and a 3-field payload is 2,715,022 B (-90.8%).
Q5 SSR adds ZERO — nuxt.config.ts:443 sets '/dashboard/**': { ssr: false }; /dashboard returns an identical 10,688-byte empty shell with AND without a session cookie (TTFB 0.09-0.17 s). useServerSessionVerify in middleware/dashboard.ts is dead code on this route.

CAUSAL PROOF (not inference): trimming only the /workspaces/all response to 50 rows via route interception, interleaved x2 against uncapped controls, drops the longest main-thread block from 4,146/4,728 ms to 132/166 ms (-96.5%) and total blocking from 6,679/5,117 ms to 336/290 ms (-94.6%).

BONUS CORRECTNESS BUG found while measuring: the 29.6 MB store write hits Chrome's ~5 MB localStorage quota, throws QuotaExceededError, and pinia-plugin-persistedstate swallows it silently (debug unset; page console logged zero errors). Consequently all 22 persisted fields of the workspace store — currentWorkspace, workspaceUser, entitlement* — stop being persisted for super admins from the moment /dashboard is opened. Capping the payload makes the write succeed.

close_reason:

ROOT CAUSE — narrower than the brief's hypothesis, and it explains the prod DB state exactly. IdeaChatPanel.vue submitGenerationBrief: an idea session enters the post-brief branch via `variant === 'idea'` with NO improvement mode (an idea chat never answers the three-mode question), and the scope it passed read `mode === 'refilm' ? undefined : 'no_refilm'`, so a null mode fell through to no_refilm. It is NOT a Post Brief mode selection leaking: pendingBriefMode is only ever set in onSelectMode, which is Make It Better-chooser-only. That is why the prod item had seed.improvementScope='default' (select-improvement-scope was never called) while the generate body carried 'no_refilm'. The brief's "second brief-submit handler ~L645" does not exist on staging tip; there is one.

FIX — durable guard at the composable seam (useIdeaChat), the single funnel every scope-carrying call passes through. It takes the chat's variant and tracks the persisted session.mode; supportsNoRefilm treats session mode as canonical once known, falls back to variant before the session loads, and stays permissive when neither is stated, so it only ever removes a known-bad send. generatePhase strips improvementScope='no_refilm' from a session that cannot carry it; selectImprovementMode AND selectImprovementScope withhold the request entirely, because that endpoint rejects every scope on a non-MIB session, not just no_refilm (idea-chat.service.ts:2285). The panel is fixed at source too, so the idea flow reads as scope-free rather than relying on the strip. Backend: assertImprovementScopeAllowed() runs the same two rules BEFORE creditsService.debit in the generate handler, reading item.ideaChatMode (equal by construction to session.mode there), and costs no extra read when no scope is requested.

task_title: Everyone who opens the payment form leaves without typing a card
close_reason:
VERDICT: PRICE, not a broken form and not Instagram. Investigation only — no code changed (execution_note=additive-only); three follow-up tasks filed instead.

WHERE THEY ABANDON — at the price, with a working form in front of them. On 28 July, of 84 payment forms that rendered, 76 asked for $99/month USD charged today, 8 asked for $29, and not one showed a trial or discount. Five people submitted a payment. Device/browser breakdown is in the discovery note: a phone funnel (Mobile Safari/iOS 50, Chrome/Android 27, 9 desktop of 88 opens).

THREE INDEPENDENT CONTROLS, ALL AGREEING:
- Over time: platform submit rate ran 20-35% of checkout opens 9-27 July, then fell to 5% on 28 July — while the form still rendered for 84 of 98. Nothing broke; the audience changed.
- Same day, same code: campaign traffic converted 1 of 45 (2.2%) once the form rendered; non-campaign 3 of 20 (15%).
- Replays: reconstructed session streams show people sitting on the form 13-31s then leaving. One (Mexico) left checkout and immediately ran three more free audits. Three replay links in the note, retained to 27 August.

INSTAGRAM IN-APP BROWSER — DISPROVEN as the checkout cause, and checked properly rather than by browser name. PostHog reports it as "Mobile Safari"/"Chrome" so a $browser breakdown shows zero Instagram; via $raw_user_agent, 18 of 65 campaign checkout-openers were inside Instagram and it rendered the form BETTER than the rest (78% vs 66%). No real-device reproduction attached because that AC was conditional on the in-app browser being the cause. It IS breaking /start on both platforms (16 people in 2 days, 100% Instagram) — filed as cas-e6fa, upstream of checkout and invisible in this task's numbers.

SECOND, SEPARATE LEAK FOUND — 31% of campaign visitors (about 20% platform-wide, chronic) opened checkout and no form ever rendered. They waited: 17 of 23 stayed 10s+, 9 over two minutes. Not the backend — subscription_checkout_failed fires on exactly that and fired zero times. Root-caused to four silent dead ends in StripeCheckoutInline.vue (bare returns at 178 and 249, un-emitted errors at 182-191, no timeout on loadStripe) plus two sequential round trips in CheckoutPanel.onMounted. Filed as cas-8a6b.

CORRECTION TO THIS TASK'S OWN PREMISE: the "zero card entry" framing rested on Stripe-side data alone. The frontend has its own funnel and it shows most of these people did reach a working card form. Also subscription_payment_details_started is mislabelled — bound to the Stripe element's @ready (mount complete), not card entry — and there is no card-entry event at all. Anything reading it as intent is wrong.

FIX PROPOSED WITH REVENUE — ranked in the second decision note. Headline: the audit paywall defaults to $99 and deliberately withholds the free-first-month option the pricing page already offers (AuditUnlockModal.vue:158). Moving this cohort from 1.5% to 4% at the payment step is ~1.6 extra subscriptions/day (~$1.4k-$4.8k MRR added per campaign month); reaching non-campaign's 8.7% would be ~4.7/day, which I would not promise. Filed as cas-2460 (P0). The render-failure fix is worth well under one sub/day and is proposed on correctness grounds, stated as such rather than dressed up as revenue.

Two learnings stored: in-app-browser detection via $raw_user_agent, and the real semantics of each checkout funnel event.

task_title: Customers whose card fails are locked out immediately and never told why
close_reason:
Investigation only, no code changed (execution_note=additive-only). All four acceptance criteria answered; three come back the opposite way to the task's framing.

1. RETRIES ARE CONFIGURED AND RUNNING — proven, not assumed. All 17 past_due subs carry auto_advance=true and a next_payment_attempt scheduled in the FUTURE (30 Jul - 3 Aug), attempt_count 1 (one at 2), billing_reason=subscription_cycle on all 17 so these are genuine renewals. The "four days of silence" is exactly the shape of Stripe's retry schedule — next attempt lands 5-8 days after the first failure. The cycle also demonstrably completes: of the 3 subs in all history that finished a past_due cycle, 1 recovered to active after 5.3 days and 2 cancelled after 5.2.
   NOT PROVEN, and I will not assert it either way: whether Stripe's customer-facing failed-payment email toggle is on. That is a Dashboard setting absent from webhook payloads. Thirty-second check, and it should be done first because it changes whether anything needs building.

2. NOTHING ON OUR SIDE CHASES THEM — your prior was right here. handlePaymentFailed (billing.service.ts:5466) retrieves the sub, invalidates cache, logs a warning, and carries the comment "Here you could send a payment failure notification, suspend features, etc." Zero payment-failure handling across /email, /crm and /sms; no billing template exists; no cron. Our own SMS channel holds their verified phone and stays silent.

3. ENTITLEMENT IS CORRECT, and too harsh. past_due is excluded from ACCESS_GATING_SUBSCRIPTION_STATUSES (billing.service.ts:375), which hasActiveSubscription evaluates at line 605; handlePaymentFailed invalidates cache immediately, so lockout is instant. None of the 17 holds a promo bypass. We are NOT giving the product away — the inverse. A customer who paid last month loses access within minutes while Stripe keeps trying to collect for another week, and we tell them nothing.
   SELF-CORRECTION: my first grep suggested that constant was defined but unused, which would have been a serious hole. My error — it is used at line 605. No hole.

4. REVENUE IS NOT INFLATED. conversion-funnel.sql computes revenue as min(received_at) FILTER (status='active') — a first-conversion count a past_due sub cannot re-enter. billing-pulse carries past_due as its own mutually exclusive census bucket.

5. THE 22% IS WRONG — it is a double count, and the true figure is the best month on record. The "29 failures" on 24 July is 15 invoice.payment_failed plus 14 payment_intent.payment_failed; I checked the overlap via payment_details.order_reference and all 14 reference invoices that also produced an invoice.payment_failed — zero unique. Same failures counted twice against a singly-counted denominator. True renewal batch: 98 paid / 14 failed = 12.5%. By month (subscription_cycle only): Feb 57.9%, Mar 63.6%, Apr 57.1%, May 46.2%, Jun 28.6%, Jul 13.5%. Five consecutive months of improvement. Caveat stated: Feb-Jun denominators are 14-22 renewals and individually noisy; July rests on 178. No shipped code double-counts — billing-pulse's payment_intent usage is correctly scoped to metadata.type='credit_pack'. The error was in this task's analysis, not the product.

RECOVERABLE REVENUE — $1,473/month exposure (14 x $99 + 3 x $29). I deliberately did NOT give a recovery figure: Stripe's retries will recover some of it unaided, which cannot be claimed as a fix's benefit, and our entire history holds 3 completed dunning cycles (1 recovered, 2 cancelled). n=3 supports neither a recovery rate nor an incremental lift; any number I quoted would be an industry benchmark wearing our logo. The current cycle completes ~3 August — measuring these 17 then gives the first cohort large enough to mean anything, and turns the question into an answered one inside a week.

IS IT JUST DEAD CARDS? Partly, and honestly yes for a share of them — the collection machinery is not broken and this is not an incident. What is not ordinary is that customers are locked out instantly and never told why. Retitle suggested: "Customers whose card fails are locked out immediately and never told why."

FIX SIZED, NOT BUILT, per your instruction: (1) check the Stripe dunning-email toggle — 30s, no code, likely the whole fix; (2) turn it on if off — no code; (3) our own email+SMS — ~1 day, only if (1) shows Stripe is silent; (4) grace period for past_due — mechanically one Set entry but a POLICY call that hands the product to dead cards for a week and collides with cas-d80b credit-wipe; needs Daniel, not a worker. task_title: Instagram's in-app browser breaks the start page — the app never loads
close_reason:
MERGED at 66a9541c2 and verified: `git merge-base --is-ancestor 69fd33724 <epic>` returns true, epic tip is 66a9541c2.

ROOT CAUSE — not Instagram, not device-specific, and the browser was never the variable. Nuxt 4 defaults `experimental.entryImportMap` to true (@nuxt/schema index.mjs:862). StableEntryPlugin (@nuxt/vite-builder index.mjs:780) then rewrites every entry-chunk reference to the bare specifier `#entry`, and the SSR renderer emits `<script type="importmap">` to resolve it — a caching optimisation whose price is that the app requires import-map support to boot at all. Nuxt's own support table (same file, line 831) names exactly those versions, and the plugin auto-disables when a `vite.build.target` below that line is declared; we declared no target, so the guard never fired.

task_title: web-fallback endpoint: require proof-of-phone-control (public unauth route grants free audits + enables phone-spoofing)
close_reason:
Free-audit mint budget on per-IP + global daily axes (non-fabricable), charged only on actual mint, all fail-closed; 8 red pre-change tests; jest 802 + bootstrap-smoke green. AC3 met; AC1/AC2 void per ruling; spoofed-phone half → cas-d690.

DETAIL FOR THE RECORD.

The defect: poc.service.ts:315 grants any workspace with owner===null && !hasReceivedFreeAudit one free PAID audit for its lifetime, and sms-responder.service.ts:879 skips the affordability pre-check on the same condition. The public @Public() web-fallback route mints exactly such a workspace for any phone string it has not seen, so the real economic bound was ONE FREE PAID AUDIT PER DISTINCT PHONE STRING — an identity the attacker mints for free by inventing an E.164 string. The pre-existing per-phone limit therefore capped an axis the attacker owns: a speed limit, not a cap. The window counters bounded the rate and never the total.

The fix: a mint budget on per-IP-per-day (WEB_FALLBACK_MINT_IP_DAILY_MAX, default 3) and GLOBAL-per-day (WEB_FALLBACK_MINT_GLOBAL_DAILY_MAX, default 200). Charged ONLY when the submission would actually mint — the phone has neither an existing workspace nor an existing account, mirroring the two skip conditions in ensureWorkspaceForPhoneUnowned. Every other property follows from that exemption: a returning submitter is never charged, so exhausting the global budget pauses NEW mints and cannot lock out anyone already in the funnel; the per-IP cap is checked FIRST and short-circuits WITHOUT touching the global counter, so one capped IP cannot drain the day's budget and take the non-US funnel down with it; a malformed phone is not charged, so garbage is not a cheap way to exhaust the cap. Both counters and the eligibility lookup FAIL CLOSED (503). Enforced in the GUARD, before the handler, so a refused submission leaves no CRM lead, no sms_messages row, no workspace. It runs after the window limits deliberately — it costs up to two indexed DB reads and an unauthenticated caller must not be able to aim those at the database at will. A global-cap bind logs at ERROR; legitimate volume is ~19 new phones/day (562 submissions / 552 distinct phones over 30d), so 200/day is ~10x headroom and a bind means attack or growth.

REUSE, NOT A SECOND MECHANISM (the supervisor's reconciliation instruction): this adds NO new proof-of-identity primitive and does not touch cas-57f1's claim path. cas-57f1's server-issued signed claim token remains the possession proof; cas-0070 adds only the mint-path cost cap, which cas-57f1's own note assigned here ("Minting is separately capped by cas-0070"). No OTP, no country-dependent SMS wall, so Daniel's cas-e8c6 ruling is untouched and no international friction is reintroduced.

Deliberately NOT touched: debitPostAudit's per-workspace lifetime grant also serves the real inbound-SMS funnel; narrowing it there would change behaviour for users this task is not about.

The 8 red are the evidence — per-IP cap, global-not-charged-after-IP-refusal, global cap, under-both-caps charges both axes, day bucketing, fail-closed on lookup, fail-closed on counter, non-positive-cap config rejection. task_title: Beth Barbeau logged out every ~10 minutes WHILE actively working on a video from the text flow

ROOT CAUSE. Two structural defects in AUTOMATIC session teardown — neither is a timer, and there is no ten-minute anything in the product.

D1: clearAllSessions() called the backend logout with no argument. The backend revokes unless told literally {revoke:false}, and revokeUserSessions(uid) kills every refresh token the account holds on every device and invalidates the 14-day session cookie (verified checkRevoked=true). Every caller of clearAllSessions is automatic — the hourly revalidation tick, the visibility handler, the page-load stale-session plugin, and initializeAuth's already-initialized recovery branch reached from every route guard. So one transient blip — Firebase losing its IndexedDB connection in an iOS webview, which this repo already documents at auth-persistence.ts:78-82 — permanently destroyed the silent re-mint that exists to keep a user signed in. It was self-sustaining: after a revoke the next forced refresh throws auth/user-token-expired, which is in REVOCATION_CODES, which calls clearAllSessions, which revokes again. The backend's own comment already warns of exactly this loop; handleTokenExpiry was given {revoke:false} for that reason and clearAllSessions never was. Revocation is now opt-in — a global irreversible action should not be what you get when nobody thought about it — and the one caller that means "log out everywhere", the sign-out button, states it. Side effect worth knowing: exiting impersonation no longer revokes the impersonated CUSTOMER's tokens on all their devices.

D2: the public SMS audit page /audit/<postId>?s=<token> — the customer's exact entry path — was guarded only inside handleTokenExpiry, whose comment calls itself "the single chokepoint every caller funnels through". It is not. clearAllSessions redirected to /sign-in from anywhere outside an exact-match allowlist that /audit was never on, so recoverStaleSession and the stale-session plugin could throw a customer working from a texted link out to the sign-in screen. Both paths now share one predicate, prefix-guarded so /audits (the signed-in list page, which should redirect) is not swallowed.

Completed-audit URL dedupe. The dedupe hit short-circuits before debitPostAudit, so "free" is structural rather than a special case in the billing path. Outside the window, or with explicit forceReaudit intent, a fresh charged audit runs. Failed runs stay re-submittable throughout, so a retry after a failure always starts a fresh run. The cache read IS the throttle — dynamoDb.get returns null past maxAge, so an entry older than the window is indistinguishable from no entry and both mean go. No new keys or storage semantics, and because the window lives in the shared DynamoDB entry the cap holds ACROSS API instances rather than per-process, which is what makes it worth anything on serverless. A genuine config change still bursts through inside the window: a cached payload built from a price ID we no longer sell fails the pre-existing freshness check and refetches regardless of age. SINGLE FLIGHT keyed by the RESOLVED market, not the request's country string. task_title: web-fallback endpoint: require proof-of-phone-control (public unauth route grants free audits + enables phone-spoofing)

DETAIL FOR THE RECORD.

The defect: poc.service.ts:315 grants any workspace with owner===null && !hasReceivedFreeAudit one free PAID audit for its lifetime, and sms-responder.service.ts:879 skips the affordability pre-check on the same condition. The public @Public() web-fallback route mints exactly such a workspace for any phone string it has not seen, so the real economic bound was ONE FREE PAID AUDIT PER DISTINCT PHONE STRING — an identity the attacker mints for free by inventing an E.164 string. The pre-existing per-phone limit therefore capped an axis the attacker owns: a speed limit, not a cap. The window counters bounded the rate and never the total.

The fix: a mint budget on per-IP-per-day (WEB_FALLBACK_MINT_IP_DAILY_MAX, default 3) and GLOBAL-per-day (WEB_FALLBACK_MINT_GLOBAL_DAILY_MAX, default 200). Charged ONLY when the submission would actually mint — the phone has neither an existing workspace nor an existing account, mirroring the two skip conditions in ensureWorkspaceForPhoneUnowned. Every other property follows from that exemption: a returning submitter is never charged, so exhausting the global budget pauses NEW mints and cannot lock out anyone already in the funnel; the per-IP cap is checked FIRST and short-circuits WITHOUT touching the global counter, so one capped IP cannot drain the day's budget and take the non-US funnel down with it; a malformed phone is not charged, so garbage is not a cheap way to exhaust the cap. Both counters and the eligibility lookup FAIL CLOSED (503). Enforced in the GUARD, before the handler, so a refused submission leaves no CRM lead, no sms_messages row, no workspace. It runs after the window limits deliberately — it costs up to two indexed DB reads and an unauthenticated caller must not be able to aim those at the database at will. A global-cap bind logs at ERROR; legitimate volume is ~19 new phones/day (562 submissions / 552 distinct phones over 30d), so 200/day is ~10x headroom and a bind means attack or growth.

REUSE, NOT A SECOND MECHANISM (the supervisor's reconciliation instruction): this adds NO new proof-of-identity primitive and does not touch cas-57f1's claim path. cas-57f1's server-issued signed claim token remains the possession proof; cas-0070 adds only the mint-path cost cap, which cas-57f1's own note assigned here ("Minting is separately capped by cas-0070"). task_title: web-fallback endpoint: require proof-of-phone-control (public unauth route grants free audits + enables phone-spoofing)
close_reason:
Free-audit mint budget on per-IP + global daily axes (non-fabricable), charged only on actual mint, all fail-closed; 8 red pre-change tests; jest 802 + bootstrap-smoke green. AC3 met; AC1/AC2 void per ruling; spoofed-phone half → cas-d690.

DETAIL FOR THE RECORD.

The defect: poc.service.ts:315 grants any workspace with owner===null && !hasReceivedFreeAudit one free PAID audit for its lifetime, and sms-responder.service.ts:879 skips the affordability pre-check on the same condition. The public @Public() web-fallback route mints exactly such a workspace for any phone string it has not seen, so the real economic bound was ONE FREE PAID AUDIT PER DISTINCT PHONE STRING — an identity the attacker mints for free by inventing an E.164 string. The pre-existing per-phone limit therefore capped an axis the attacker owns: a speed limit, not a cap. The window counters bounded the rate and never the total.

The fix: a mint budget on per-IP-per-day (WEB_FALLBACK_MINT_IP_DAILY_MAX, default 3) and GLOBAL-per-day (WEB_FALLBACK_MINT_GLOBAL_DAILY_MAX, default 200). Charged ONLY when the submission would actually mint — the phone has neither an existing workspace nor an existing account, mirroring the two skip conditions in ensureWorkspaceForPhoneUnowned. Every other property follows from that exemption: a returning submitter is never charged, so exhausting the global budget pauses NEW mints and cannot lock out anyone already in the funnel; the per-IP cap is checked FIRST and short-circuits WITHOUT touching the global counter, so one capped IP cannot drain the day's budget and take the non-US funnel down with it; a malformed phone is not charged, so garbage is not a cheap way to exhaust the cap. Both counters and the eligibility lookup FAIL CLOSED (503). Enforced in the GUARD, before the handler, so a refused submission leaves no CRM lead, no sms_messages row, no workspace. It runs after the window limits deliberately — it costs up to two indexed DB reads and an unauthenticated caller must not be able to aim those at the database at will. A global-cap bind logs at ERROR; legitimate volume is ~19 new phones/day (562 submissions / 552 distinct phones over 30d), so 200/day is ~10x headroom and a bind means attack or growth.

REUSE, NOT A SECOND MECHANISM (the supervisor's reconciliation instruction): this adds NO new proof-of-identity primitive and does not touch cas-57f1's claim path. cas-57f1's server-issued signed claim token remains the possession proof; cas-0070 adds only the mint-path cost cap, which cas-57f1's own note assigned here ("Minting is separately capped by cas-0070"). No OTP, no country-dependent SMS wall, so Daniel's cas-e8c6 ruling is untouched and no international friction is reintroduced.

Deliberately NOT touched: debitPostAudit's per-workspace lifetime grant also serves the real inbound-SMS funnel; narrowing it there would change behaviour for users this task is not about.

EVIDENCE, no proxy checks. New src/sms/web-fallback-rate-limit.guard.spec.ts (the guard had NO unit spec before). Against the PRE-change guard: 8 failed, 6 passed, 14 total. The 8 red are the evidence — per-IP cap, global-not-charged-after-IP-refusal, global cap, under-both-caps charges both axes, day bucketing, fail-closed on lookup, fail-closed on counter, non-positive-cap config rejection. Stated rather than counted: the 3 exemption/malformed cases passed pre-change VACUOUSLY (no mint keys existed to touch) and the 3 window cases are regression pins. Post-change 14/14. Per-worktree deps (pnpm install --frozen-lockfile exit 0, npx prisma generate exit 0, no symlinks to the main checkout): tsc --noEmit clean; jest src/sms src/workspaces --runInBand → 59 suites / 802 tests; full unit suite 290/291 suites and 4071/4072 tests, the single failure (conversion-sms-enroll "sets absolute expectedAt from enroll") PROVEN pre-existing by stashing the whole diff and re-running at the base — identical failure, wall-clock-shaped assertion in a file this diff does not touch; nest build + scripts/bootstrap-smoke-test.js exit 0, "dependencies resolved (59 modules)", which is what proves the new PrismaService injection into a guard is wired since hand-constructed unit guards would not catch bad DI; eslint 0 errors on all touched files.

THE DEFECT. users.service.ts auto-joined a signing-up user to EVERY workspace holding a PENDING invite for their email, with no expiry filter — so an invite dead for months still granted membership, project access and an ACCEPTED stamp. The mirror image of cas-06da (dead row blocks re-invite); this is the dead row treated as alive. The two read paths disagreed and this was the lenient half: workspace-roles.service.ts:360-366 getPendingInvitationsByEmail has always filtered expirationDatetime > now(). They now agree.

THE PRODUCT QUESTION THIS TASK WAS PARKED ON WAS SETTLED BY MEASUREMENT, not taste. The concern on file was that filtering "silently stops onboarding people who sign up >7 days after being invited". Measured against PROD (wispy-voice-65668735): every workspace_invite row in history — 17 rows back to 2025-11-06 — left-joined to accounts on lower(email) and bucketed on whether the account was created after its invite expired:
  - signed up AFTER expiry: 0
  - signed up inside the window: 8, nearly all the SAME DAY as the invite
  - no account yet: 9
  - totals: 13 PENDING (7 currently expired), 4 ACCEPTED
That cohort has never existed in this product, which is what removed the only reason options (b) extend-expiry-on-accept and (c) lengthen-TTL were on the table. Supervisor ruled option (a) on this evidence and explicitly kept TTL length as a separate, optional product question for Daniel — not a prerequisite. The commit records that if volume ever changes, the lever is the 7-day TTL in workspace.service.ts:1408, NOT reopening this filter, which is what keeps the two paths agreeing.

SECOND DEFECT, same update, found while measuring and folded in on the supervisor's explicit instruction rather than split: the accept stamped status=ACCEPTED but never acceptedAt, so a row recorded THAT an invite was accepted and never WHEN. 3 of the 4 ACCEPTED rows in prod carry accepted_at = NULL — which is exactly why "was this accepted after it expired?" could not be read off the row and had to be triangulated through accounts.createdAt. Now stamped.

EVIDENCE — 4 tests red pre-change in users.service.spec.ts. They use an HONEST workspaceInvite.findMany double that really applies the `where` it is handed, so they assert the resulting MEMBERSHIP rather than the shape of a query object — a test that merely pattern-matched the filter would have passed with the filter applied to the wrong field. Both debit sites call it BEFORE the debit — afterwards the consumption row exists either way and the question is unanswerable — and return `charged` alongside the draft item. The debit calls themselves are unchanged, so there is no behaviour change to the ledger path.

Why not reuse the existing `resumed` flag: it is false whenever the draft item is gone even if the consumption row survives (still a free call), and false when enforcement is off and nothing is charged at all. A test pins that distinction so nobody collapses the two later.

CLIENT. useWorkingDraftItem exposes lastCreateCharged; the audit page debits only when true. Three paths set it false, each documented in place: a missing `charged` field (older backend deploy), a failed create, and the short-circuit where a confirmed draft means no request goes out. The asymmetry is deliberate — under-debiting is corrected by the authoritative refresh a second later, over-debiting is the bug being fixed.

A confirmed draft item is exactly the condition under which the server takes its no-charge resume branch, so a low balance is irrelevant there and no new client state was needed. task_title: audit page watcher fires on every store update — add concurrency guard
close_reason:
Coalesce audit-page silent refreshes: primitive postId:status watch key + coalescing runner (queue-one, not drop) + loading-watch drain for the first-load race; 10 same-status emits → 1 fetch, real-store RED/GREEN, 1991 tests green.

Root cause was sharper than the ticket had it: the watcher source was the PostUpdate OBJECT, and applyUpdates overwrites on `updatedAt >=` — note >=, not >. Every poll tick that re-reports the post installs a brand-new object with identical contents, so a reference watch re-fires on each cursor-driven re-emit. Never really about status filtering; object identity churned on every emit.

Did BOTH options the ticket offered, since AC1 and AC2 are separate requirements. Option 2: watch `${postId}:${status}`, a primitive, so Vue dedupes by value; postId in the key so switching between two posts sharing a status is not swallowed. Option 1: every silent refresh routes through createCoalescedRefresh, which serialises passes — relevant because there are TWO independent silent callers, this watcher and a 5s processing poll, so a fetch slower than the interval could be overtaken.

Coalesce, not drop: a request landing mid-flight may reflect a status that did not exist when the in-flight fetch was issued, so discarding it strands the page on a stale status at the final transition. One follow-up pass is sufficient and bounded (burst of N → 1).

Two further holes closed while wiring it: (a) the runner drains its own queue when one of ITS passes settles, but a request deferred by the non-silent initial load has no such pass to wait on — added a watch(loading) drain, else a transition arriving during first load hangs forever on an audit with no processing poll; (b) starting a pass must clear `queued`, else an isBusy-deferred request fires a redundant second pass.

Helpers live in utils/post-refresh.ts so they are testable: the page is ~1300 lines wired to Quasar/Nuxt/PostHog, mounting it to count fetches is mostly stub-wrangling, and source-text assertions pin the code we happened to write rather than the behaviour.

All 3 ACs met, AC3 verbatim (1 real transition + 9 same-status re-emits → exactly 1 call). Tests use the REAL Pinia store and REAL Vue watch. Verified RED against the pre-fix source expression: 10 fires where the fix gives 1.

task_title: Staging E2E: no working browser-auth seeding path for service-account-minted Firebase tokens — document/build one
close_reason:
Merged as 14cc6fe73 and promoted to staging.

Committed token-auth E2E seeding path (tests/config/token-auth.ts): mint a service-account Firebase token → write Firebase's own IndexedDB record before the app boots → reload. No password anywhere, no product-code change, no test-only route added to the app. Key/db/store names taken from @firebase/auth 1.10.8's own _persistenceKeyName/DB_NAME constants rather than guessed.

Proven live against deployed staging three times (2 passed, 16.2s / 16.0s / 15.5s, headless): the signed-in shell renders staging-admin@gabber.studio on /admin/analytics, with a NEGATIVE CONTROL in the same spec proving an unseeded browser is bounced off that route and holds no Firebase user.

That control exists because my first version was a worthless proxy check: it passed while the seeded session had silently bounced to /sign-in, since an anonymous browser renders the admin page's static labels anyway. Caught by probing the rendered text instead of trusting green.

Four traps measured and encoded: page.goto() on a guarded route redirects (SSR cannot see a token in browser IndexedDB); addInitScript cannot block an async IndexedDB write, so the write happens on a cheap same-origin page followed by a reload; `node -e <code> a b c` shifts process.argv by one and reading the env file from the wrong slot surfaces as firebase-admin INVALID_CREDENTIAL, which reads like bad keys rather than a bad path; apps/frontend/.env's web API key is stale and a git worktree has no .env at all (hence the live-bundle scrape and GABBER_BACKEND_ENV_FILE).

Rewrote staging-verify §3b, which had delegated the recipe to the cas-nuxt-playwright skill that is not installed in this repo — part of why this stayed unsolved. It now names the committed helper, gives the runnable command, lists the four traps, and warns against asserting on page text.
