close_reason:
NOT REPRODUCIBLE at staging 2157a237c. Investigation-only; no code changed by design.

MEASURED, not assumed:
- `pnpm dev` on the main checkout boots (Nitro 1451ms, Vite client+server built), prints `➜ Local: http://localhost:3000/`, and curl returns HTTP 200. Ran the full 180s to a clean timeout kill (exit 124). Zero hits for `assertion`, `RemoveEnvironmentCleanupHook`, `hooks.cc`, `Aborted` or `core dumped` in the log. The task's stated impact — "no local E2E/dev-server verification possible for any worker" — is false today; the Vercel-deploy workaround is not needed on that account.
- better-sqlite3 12.4.1 exercised directly: require → open :memory: → prepare/get → close → clean exit; exit-without-close; and worker-thread load + teardown (the usual trigger for a cleanup-hook abort) — all clean, exit 0. Same result inside a factory worktree install (patient-jay-87), so it is not worktree-specific.
- No ABI mismatch on the active runtime: the module declares engines.node "20.x || 22.x || 23.x || 24.x", is built from source (build/Release present, no prebuilds dir), and is compiled for NODE_MODULE_VERSION 137 = active node v24.19.0. Verified working on v24.19.0 and v24.15.0.

The task's hypothesis (prebuilt-binary ABI mismatch) is therefore disproven. Stated explicitly because it matters for any recurrence: a genuine ABI mismatch raises a clean JS ERR_DLOPEN_FAILED ("compiled against NODE_MODULE_VERSION 137 / requires 127", reproduced under node v22.22.2) — NOT the `Assertion failed: (env) != nullptr` native abort in the report. So the named mechanism does not produce the reported signature, and I could not induce that abort by any route tried.

LATENT DIVERGENCE FOUND, deliberately left unfixed: the repo standardizes on Node 20 (.nvmrc = 20; all 6 CI workflows pin node-version 20) while this machine runs v24.19.0 with Node 20 not installed at all (only 22.12.0, 22.22.2, 24.15.0, 24.19.0). So `nvm use` per the repo's own convention cannot succeed here, and anyone landing on Node 22 breaks every native module. Node 20 also hit EOL 2026-04-30. This is the most plausible origin of the 2026-08-17 report. Aligning .nvmrc and the CI pins is deploy-affecting (Vercel + 6 workflows) and is Daniel's call, not a P3 worker's unilateral edit — flagged to the supervisor for a separate task.

Recovery runbook, if the abort ever recurs: compare `node -p process.versions.modules` against the ABI in build/Release/better_sqlite3.node, then rebuild from source against the active runtime with `pnpm rebuild better-sqlite3` — reinstalling will not help, as there are no prebuilds to fall back to.

Merged into epic/epic-create-conversational-workspace-remediation-b-cas-397c @ fbbaa97e1 (supervisor merge of factory/brave-salmon-78 @ 99edfd651). Verified reachable — `git merge-base --is-ancestor 99edfd651 fbbaa97e1` passes, the diff on the epic tip is exactly the 282 insertions / 11 deletions I authored, and all four new symbols (stripAcknowledgmentLabel, reflectionFromMessage, capAtWordBoundary, SURVIVING_FIRST_PERSON) are present there. Backend only; frontend untouched (`git diff --stat -- apps/frontend` empty).

(a) LABEL — fixed on BOTH sides deliberately, because a prompt is a request and not a guarantee, and either fix alone leaves the other side able to reintroduce the defect. The system prompt now says "Reply with the sentences only, with no label — never begin with 'acknowledgment:', 'ack:', 'reflection:' or 'intent:'", AND `stripAcknowledgmentLabel()` removes a leading role/format label on the way out, including markdown-emphasised and en/em-dash variants. Strip rather than reject: the sentence AFTER the label was perfectly good, and rejecting would have thrown it away for the generic static line, losing the content-aware first beat A2 exists to provide. `isUsableAcknowledgment` additionally refuses any content still matching the label prefix, so a variant slipping past the stripper cannot render. START-anchored, so "the intent is to explore concept directions" survives as ordinary prose — pinned by its own test, because a greedy strip would have eaten exactly the good half of the observed reply.

(b) TIMEOUT — the reflection is BUILT, not echoed. First-person desire opener removed ("i want to do a post on X" → "a post on X"); removal rather than substituting "a", because the object already brings its own article and substitution yields "a a post". Possessives flipped (my→your, me→you). First clause only. Capped at 90 chars on a word boundary with an ellipsis, with the full stop suppressed after "…" so there is no "…." seam. Anything that would still speak AS the creator drops the reflection entirely and ships the intent statement alone — losing the content beat is the lesser harm against parroting, which is the whole complaint. Gabber's OWN first person ("i'll sketch…") is correct and untouched.

TWO THINGS I GOT WRONG AND CORRECTED — both are the interesting part of this task:
1. My first version of the first-person test asserted `not.toMatch(/\bi\b/)` on the whole result. That matches Gabber's own "i'll", so the assertion was wrong, not the code. Corrected to assert the exact intended output.
2. My first CLAUSE_BOUNDARY included `:`, which turned "post idea: a roofing storm-damage reveal" into "got it — post idea." — keeping the label and discarding the content, strictly worse than the parroting being fixed. THE SUITE WAS FULLY GREEN while this was true; I found it only by probing a realistic input shape rather than trusting green. `:` removed, test added. Conjunctions are excluded for the same class of reason (" and " would amputate "strengths and weaknesses", one noun phrase).

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- A model reply beginning with "acknowledgment:" and similar never reaches the thread: stripped to the sentence. Primary test uses the verbatim walk string; plus 8 label variants (Acknowledgment / acknowledgement / ACK / "ack - " / Reflection / Intent / **Acknowledgment:** / *intent*:), a label-only reply falling back to the deterministic line, and a prose-"intent" negative guard.
- Timeout fallback is second-person, ≤~90 chars cut at a word boundary with an ellipsis, never a first-person verbatim echo: tested on Ben's opening message (exact expected string) and a long direction message (ellipsis, word boundary, substring-of-original, no "…." seam), plus 4 opener shapes, the my→your flip, one-clause-only, and the drop-entirely guard.
- Existing ack tests green: yes — and verified AT RED that zero pre-existing tests were failing, so nothing was "fixed" by moving a goalpost.
- Suites + typecheck green with real exit codes: below.

RED-FIRST: 23 tests written and run before implementation, 19 red. The 4 that passed at red are deliberate guards on behaviour that already held (a label-only reply already fell back; "intent" as prose was already safe) — regression protection, not padding.

MUTATION-TESTED — every component proven load-bearing by disabling each in turn and counting what breaks:
| component disabled | tests that fail |
| label stripper + reject guard | 9 |
| first-person opener strip | 8 |
| clause cut | 3 |
| surviving-first-person guard | 1 |
| my/me → your/you flip | 1 |
| prompt "no label" instruction | 1 |
No dead code, no vacuous assertions. File byte-compared identical to the fixed version afterwards.

VERIFICATION — exit codes captured from each command directly, on the merged tree:
| jest src/items/idea-chat | 0 | 36 suites, 570/570 (baseline 569 before my 24) |
| tsc --noEmit (backend) | 0 | 0 errors |
| eslint (2 changed files) | 0 | 0 errors |
| prettier --check | 0 | clean |

HONEST LIMITS: both defects were observed on staging; the fixes are proven only in-tree. (a) is deterministic and fully covered. (b) is deterministic too, but only renders when the 1.1s timeout actually fires, so confirming it in a live thread needs a deployed branch build I do not control. The rewrite is also English-only: a Spanish creator's message has no "i want to" to strip, so it takes the drop-the-reflection path and receives the intent statement alone — correct, but less content-aware than the English path. Worth a follow-up only if a walk shows it mattering.

task_title: Flaky: CreditBalance.entitlement-window.test.ts fails under full-suite parallel load (5000ms timeout + duplicated fetch call), passes in isolation
close_reason:
Merged into epic/epic-create-conversational-workspace-remediation-b-cas-397c @ 1b57c8c4d (supervisor merge of factory/brave-salmon-78 @ 03030e752). Verified reachable — `git merge-base --is-ancestor 03030e752 1b57c8c4d` passes, and the file on the epic tip carries the hoisted import at line 153 with `mounted.push(wrapper)` at 157, i.e. the atomic mount/register pair that is the whole fix. Test-only: one file, 26 insertions / 1 deletion.

ROOT CAUSE — and the brief's hypothesis was wrong, which I established before moving on rather than after. The task said to bisect file order for what leaks IN. Nothing leaks in: the file poisons itself, and both reported symptoms are ONE defect.

RULED OUT FIRST: cross-file globalThis clobbering. This file does `Object.assign(globalThis, {onMounted, ...})` at module load, and two other files install a SYNCHRONOUS immediate-invoke onMounted on that same global (create.test.ts:205, workspace-hydration.test.ts:57) — a textbook candidate. Ran all three under `--no-isolate --no-file-parallelism`, one shared context with isolation fully off: 36/36 pass. Vitest never runs two files concurrently in one context, so those beforeEach writes cannot interleave. A file-order bisect would have chased this for nothing.

ACTUAL MECHANISM: `mountCounter` did slow async work BEFORE registering the wrapper for cleanup —
    const CreditBalance = (await import('~/components/CreditBalance.vue')).default;  // slow
    const wrapper = mount(...);
    mounted.push(wrapper);   // registration AFTER the await

Symptom 1 (5000ms timeout): the SFC transform sat inside the first test's budget. Measured — isolation 568ms; full parallel load 848 / 1408 / 1041ms; the other eight tests flat at 3-23ms throughout. Only the first test's duration scales with contention, because only it pays the transform. On a box busier than this idle 32-core one, breaching 5000ms is a matter of degree, not kind.

Symptom 2 ("expected 1 call, got 2") is symptom 1's collateral: a vitest timeout fails the test and runs afterEach but CANNOT cancel the promise. The abandoned continuation still mounts the component and pushes it into `mounted` after cleanup already drained the array. That orphan keeps a live watcher on the shared module-level workspaceRef, so the next test to hydrate a workspace records two loadEntitlementWindow calls.

PROVEN, NOT INFERRED. A purpose-built probe (run, then deleted — not shipped) reproduced the reported signature deterministically:
    PROBE mounted-registry size: 2
    PROBE fetches: [{"force":false,"workspaceId":"ws_1"},{"force":false,"workspaceId":"ws_1"}]
    AssertionError: expected [...] to have a length of 1 but got 2
Verbatim the bug report's second failure.

FIX: hoist the import to module load so `mount` and `mounted.push` occupy the same synchronous tick with no await between them. Kills the trigger (no transform inside a test budget) and the cascade (no suspension point where a timeout can separate a live component from its cleanup). ESM caches the module either way, so it is not a behaviour change — every test still mounts a fresh instance. The in-file comment states the invariant and warns that re-introducing an await in that gap re-introduces the flake.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- Root cause identified and documented (which state leaks and from where): above, plus a discovery note on the task. The leaked state is a live Vue watcher held by an orphaned component instance on the file's own module-level refs; the source is the file's own timed-out test, not another file.
- Full `vitest run` passes 5 consecutive times, no failures in this file: 229 files / 2514 tests, green 5/5 on the MERGED tree, 0 CreditBalance failures. Re-earned after the epic tip moved to c991db2c0 mid-task; I merged and re-ran rather than carrying the pre-merge numbers over.
- File still passes in isolation: 9/9.
- No retry/annotation-based suppression: none. No `retry`, no `.skip`, no timeout bump — the timeout is untouched at its default; the work simply no longer happens inside it.

FIX IS LOAD-BEARING — A/B, not a green-after claim:
- first test under full parallel load: 1408ms peak BEFORE → 46/42/32/28/19ms AFTER pre-merge, 39/29/30/30/28ms post-merge. ~30x, and the contention-driven variance collapses.
- with `--testTimeout=12` forced low enough to still kill test 1 on the FIXED file, every later test passes — including both that assert exactly one fetch, precisely where the pre-fix probe failed with "got 2".

ALSO SWEPT: no other test file shares the shape. Four others do `await import()` inside test bodies (auth-bootstrap, funnel-telemetry, usePostUpdatesPolling, useNonUsFallbackFlow) but none mount a component, so none can strand a live watcher on shared module state. No follow-up task needed.

VERIFICATION — exit codes captured from each command directly, on the merged tree:
| vitest run (full) x5 | 0,0,0,0,0 | 229 files, 2514/2514 each |
| vitest run (this file alone) | 0 | 9/9 |
| nuxt typecheck | 0 | 0 errors |
| eslint (changed file) | 0 | 0 errors, 0 warnings |
| prettier --check | 0 | clean |

HONEST LIMIT: the original flake never reproduced here — 5 full runs before I touched anything were green (229 files / 2507 tests each). 32 idle cores will not starve a worker the way the reporting environment did. I did not wait for a lucky red run; I measured the trigger's load sensitivity, reproduced the leak mechanism deterministically, and removed it by construction. The claim is that the mechanism is gone, not that I observed the original failure and watched it disappear.

task_title: Re-walk F3: refreshing /create loses a workspace-created draft from view — ?itemId= only resolves items with sourcePostAuditId
close_reason:
Merged into epic/epic-create-conversational-workspace-remediation-b-cas-397c @ bccc3c379 (supervisor merge of factory/brave-salmon-78 @ 2e38580f6). Verified reachable: `git merge-base --is-ancestor 2e38580f6 bccc3c379` passes, and the four files land on the epic tip with exactly the diff I authored (composable +51, create.vue +90, en.json +1, es.json +1). cas-68cc, merged in the same window, touched only backend files — `git log 028aa1d6e..bccc3c379 -- useCreativeWorkspaceConversation.ts` lists my commit alone, so there was no interaction on the shared composable. Frontend-only; no backend change was needed.

ROOT CAUSE — two independent halves, both required. The task brief named the first; the second was mine to find, and without it the first is inert.
1. create.vue:200-206 built `auditedSources` from useRecentWork filtered on `entry.sourcePostAuditId`; create.vue:259-267 resolved `route.query.itemId` ONLY against that list and fell through to `?? null` on a miss. `ensureSource` (useCreativeWorkspaceConversation.ts:917) POSTs an item with no audit, so the draft /create makes for itself could never be in the list.
2. Nothing ever wrote `?itemId=` into the URL after ensureSource, so a working resolver would still have had nothing to resolve after a first send.

FIX
- `resolveSourceById(itemId)` on the composable: GET /api/v1/workspaces/{ws}/items?itemIds=<id>&limit=1, unwrapped with the existing `unwrapListPayload`; returns {itemId, projectSlug, title} or null when the row has no project slug, so a /p/null/i/<id> route can never be synthesised. Id-only by necessity: [itemId].vue:74 links back with {path:'/create', query:{itemId}} and carries no slug, so anything needing the slug up front could not serve the return path either.
- create.vue resolution: audited list first (no request), otherwise one lookup per id guarded by `attemptedItemIds`; a throw releases the id so a transient failure stays retryable; a stale in-flight answer is dropped when routeItemId no longer matches.
- URL sync via `router.replace` (not push, so Back does not land on an itemId-less /create); preserves the rest of the query; removes itemId when the select is cleared; deliberately silent while nothing has ever been selected, or it would delete the very id being resolved.
- `sourceOptions` offers the resolved draft in the q-select so the control does not read as empty after a reload.
- New locale key `creativeWorkspace.draftSourceTitle` (en + es) names the draft on BOTH the POST and the read-back, replacing the hardcoded English 'Creative workspace draft' literal that was in ensureSource.

NO BACKEND CHANGE — verified, not assumed: workspace-items.controller.ts:187/239 already normalizes `itemIds`; items.service.ts:1325 sets where.id={in:itemIds} while KEEPING where.project.workspaceId from :1319, so the id filter cannot cross workspaces; project.slug is in the include at :1780. The same endpoint is already consumed in production by the recent-work feed.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- URL carries ?itemId=<created id> after a first send — "writes ?itemId= into the URL when the first send creates the item" asserts router.replace with the created id; a companion test asserts the rest of the query survives and itemId is dropped on clear.
- Reload re-hydrates the thread from the server session, tested with a NON-AUDITED item — covered on both layers: the page test asserts resolveSourceById is called and loadSession runs; the composable test drives the real loadSession path and asserts the transcript turn comes back.
- returnTo=creative-workspace lands on the same conversation — a test mounts with id-only query, resolves, clicks Done, and asserts push to /p/acme/i/draft-7?tab=context&returnTo=creative-workspace.
- Suites + typecheck green with real exit codes — below.

RED-FIRST: all 13 tests written and run before implementation. 6 composable tests failed with "resolveSourceById is not a function"; 6 of 7 page tests failed (resolveSourceById never called, replace never called, modelValue null). The 7th — "takes the audited list first and never asks the server for an id it already has" — passed at red on purpose; it is the regression guard on the path that already worked.

TWO THINGS WORTH CARRYING FORWARD
1. Vacuous-assertion trap, closed: the locale test would have passed with NO localization at all, because t() over en.json returns the same literal the code could have hardcoded. It now asserts the title is not the dotted key AND that es differs from en, so a missing es entry fails.
2. Dependency-resolution trap, caught late: the worktree had no root/backend node_modules, so my first verification run resolved vite/vitest/nuxt UPWARD into the main checkout's root node_modules, whose lockfile (ca88eec7…) differs from this worktree's (4890c8eb…). Every number I had reported was measured against a tree I had not proven was the right one — the proxy-check shape. I ran `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (exit 0; its success under --frozen-lockfile is itself proof the worktree lockfile matches its package.json set) and re-ran everything. All results identical, because the lockfile delta is backend-only (body-parser, express-rate-limit, eventsource) and I exercised none of it — luck in part, not design, which is why re-measuring beat reasoning about it.

| nuxt prepare | 0 | types generated |

task_title: Re-walk 2 F11: the pre-flight generation gate runs before the explicit-value lock — "change the framework to listicle and write a new script" with no framework locked returns blocked_script + framework cards instead of locking Listicle / Steps
close_reason:
F11 fixed: the explicit-value lock now resolves and applies BEFORE the pre-flight gate. Commit 6a1e32514, merged into the epic at caad40dd6. Epic tip 560ab7736 was synced first (my merge fast-forwarded to 7091ec724, which is the same tip the supervisor later named — so notification 10711 was already satisfied). 4 files, +383/-61.

Verified on the epic TREE, not just by ancestry: in the merged idea-chat.service.ts, resolveExplicitCreativeFieldLock is at line 1075 and resolveCreativeWorkspaceGenerationGate at 1104 — the order is inverted from the defect. The blocked union member carries lockedFields, and both walk-2 tests are present in the merged spec.

WHAT WAS WRONG. resolveCreativeWorkspaceGenerationGate ran at ~1044 and the lock at ~1107, so for "I actually want to change the framework to be listicle and want a new script" with framework null, the script's framework dependency was judged against a draft that did not yet contain the framework the creator had just named in the same sentence. cas-4a93 only covered the already-locked case, where the gate passed for the wrong reason. Moving the lock above the gate means the gate judges the post-lock draft and can no longer demand a dependency the same message supplies.

THE NON-OBVIOUS HALF, now a code comment so it survives the next edit. Sequencing deliberately stays on the PRE-lock draft. It decides whether a request would destroy work that already existed, and the value being written is not such work. Had I resolved it after applying the lock, targetOverwritesLockedField would see the framework just written, judge the request destructive, and defer the script behind a confirmation — turning one sentence into two turns for a creator who asked for one. Test (a) pins this: capability.generate called ONCE for scriptNotes, question null, pendingRequest null.

BLOCKED TURNS CAN NOW HAVE WRITTEN SOMETHING. "use direct to camera and write a script" locks the format and is then gated on the framework, so the blocked union member gained an optional lockedFields and the service passes it. Without it the format would change with nothing in the thread to show for it — the F9 defect reproduced on the blocked path. No client change was needed: ConversationResult.lockedFields and the appendResultTurns anchor loop built in cas-4a93 are not kind-gated, so they handled a blocked result the moment the backend began sending it.

AC BY AC.
- Lock applied before the pre-flight gate and before pending-request bookkeeping: yes, both walk cases through the real executeCreativeWorkspaceIntent. (a) framework null + the F9 message → framework locked user_provided, lockedFields ['framework'], script generated in the SAME pass, no blocked result. (b) format null + "use direct to camera and write a script" → formatType direct_to_camera + formatOptionId direct_60s written, then kind:'blocked' templateKey blocked_script with missingTargets ['framework'] and a message that does not mention the format, plus lockedFields ['formatType'].
- No stale pendingRequest replaying a dependency prompt after the lock: test (a) asserts pendingRequest is null; the frontend test asserts the resume sends 'Choose a framework' and that 'Choose a format' is never sent — the format is no longer missing, so replaying it would be the stale prompt.
- Existing F9 tests green, unmodified.

RED-FIRST EVIDENCE, stated exactly rather than rounded up.
Backend — both tests were written first and failed against the unmodified service, reproducing the staging symptom. Re-confirmed after the fix by stashing the two source files: "locks a named framework BEFORE the script gate judges the draft (walk 2 F11)" and "locks a named format first, then gates the script on what is STILL missing" both fail, 6 pass. Restored → 8/8.
Frontend — "anchors the locked receipt and resumes on the dependency that is still missing" PASSED AT RED and I am NOT counting it as red. The client already handled lockedFields on any result kind, and the test drives a mocked blocked result, so it proves the contract end-to-end but not new client behaviour. The backend change is what makes it reachable in production.

TWO THINGS THE TESTS TAUGHT ME, recorded rather than papered over.
1. Case (b) needs applyFormatEnabled: true or the format gate is not live at all — and with it true, hydrateDraftFormatFromItem runs for real and calls this.prisma.item.update. I gave the fixture a prisma stub rather than spying hydrateDraftFormatFromItem away, because the spy would have hidden the very path the test exists to exercise.
2. The first version of the frontend test asserted on raw turns and failed with 2 anchors, not 1: the mock returns the same blocked result for the original send and the resume, so the server reports the lock twice. The projector already de-dupes by field (latestReceiptAnchor), so the SCREEN was correct. I moved the assertion to conversation.threadItems — the projected thread — because "only one FORMAT receipt ever reaches the creator" is the real guarantee and a raw-turn count is not.

| backend `npx jest src/items/idea-chat` | 0 | 36 suites / 547 tests (was 543; +4) |
| backend `npx tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json` | 0 | 0 errors |
| frontend `npx vitest run` | 0 | 230 files / 2548 tests (was 2547; +1) |

That is arguably the same F9 principle, but it changes the main "Choose a format" dependency path that cas-e3b4/cas-4277 had just reworked, and neither AC asked for it. task_title: Re-walk F9: "change the framework to listicle" generates framework candidates that never render, leaves "Do This, Not That" locked, yet the confirmation claims "That's the framework updated"
close_reason:
F9 fixed in three places, in the order the defect happens. Work commits 14818ef64 (the fix) + cee75782d (supervisor guard tests), branch tip cee75782d, merged into the epic at f144b790f and 560ab7736. Verified by ancestry AND by content against the epic tree: resolveExplicitCreativeFieldLock, applyExplicitCreativeFieldLock, optionsOwnValue, the es.json multiIntentSelection key and the guard describe are all present in the merged files. 12 files, +1119/-24, plus a 21-line test-only follow-up.

AC 1 — "change the framework to listicle" locks framework="Listicle / Steps" as user_provided, receipt updates, copy is correct, deferred script waits for yes.
NEW pure module apps/backend/src/items/idea-chat/creative-workspace-explicit-value.ts: resolveExplicitCreativeFieldLock({message, targets}) matches the message against the framework catalogue (framework-options.ts) and the format catalogue (format-options.ts). Guards, each with its own test: a SET cue must be present ("change … to", "use", "switch to", "make it", "go with", "i want"); option-seeking phrasing ("options", "suggest", "a few", "what are") vetoes the lock; aliases under 5 characters are rejected (PAS/BAB/Q&A collide with ordinary prose — those stay card-only, which is unambiguous by construction); the Unknown and "Hybrid / Multiple" placeholders are never lockable; matching is word-boundary over space-padded normalized forms, longest alias wins. idea-chat.service.ts gains applyExplicitCreativeFieldLock: writes the draft through the existing applySuggestionToDraft (so a format lock still gets its formatOptionId), records the component with provenance user_provided and immediately accepts it via acceptCreativeCandidate — which is what marks the previous version superseded — locks the phase session, and pushes the value to the item column via applyDraftFieldToItem. When the whole running half of the ask was a named value, executeCreativeWorkspaceIntent returns before any audit work and never calls the capability service. When a lock is mixed with real generation, the lock is applied BEFORE the generation loop so the generation is briefed on the framework the creator chose, and its phase is filtered out of `phases`.

AC 2 — candidates generated for a locked field render, and the prior receipt shows superseded.
ROOT CAUSE, file:line: apps/frontend/app/src/utils/project-creative-workspace-thread.ts:317-345 (old) collapsed the LATEST option group for a field into a receipt whenever isCreativeDraftValueSet(field, draftValue). framework was already "Do This, Not That", so the fresh group (Listicle / Steps, Mistakes to Avoid, Unpopular Opinion, Framework Breakdown) was replaced by a receipt of the OLD value — no "Listicle" anywhere in the thread, receipt unchanged, exactly what was measured. The projector now tracks lockIndex per field: the last thing that produced the CURRENT value (the group it was picked from, or a threadReceipt anchor). A group after that index is the live question and renders as cards; the group that owns the value collapses into its receipt and is marked superseded while fresher cards are on screen. Ownership is decided by new exported optionsOwnValue, deliberately forgiving (either normalized string containing the other) so an appended or reformatted applied value still collapses — a "no" is reserved for a group that plainly has nothing to do with the locked value. The ordinary collapse grammar is pinned by an explicit regression test.

AC 3 — the confirmation never claims an update that did not persist, tested on both paths.
CreativeWorkspaceQuestionTemplateKey gains 'multi_intent_selection'. resolveCreativeWorkspaceSequencing takes lockedTargets; the first target having LOCKED is the only thing that authorizes "That's {first} updated". Otherwise the beat is "Here are a few {first} — pick one and I'll redo {rest} to match." New locale keys in en.json AND es.json: creativeWorkspace.thread.confirmation.multiIntentSelection plus a targetsPlural block (the selection beat needs a plural noun; the confirmation beat names one field). The generated result carries lockedFields; the composable appends a threadReceipt anchor per locked field — the same mechanism selectFormat already uses at useCreativeWorkspaceConversation.ts:822 — because a lock has no option group to collapse and would otherwise change the draft with nothing on screen.

DELIBERATE CHANGE TO AN EXISTING TEST. creative-workspace-execution.spec.ts "runs only the first target of a destructive multi-intent request…" used the F9 message verbatim ("Change the framework to listicle and write a new script") and asserted that the framework phase GENERATED and that the beat said multi_intent_confirmation. That test encoded the defect. Its message is now "Change the framework and write a new script" (no named value), so it still covers the D3 sequencing rule on the branch where generation is correct, and it additionally asserts multi_intent_selection and that the copy does not contain "updated". The F9 message is covered by the new test directly below it, which asserts capability.generate was never called, the draft framework is "Listicle / Steps", provenance is user_provided + accepted, framework-original is superseded, workingDraft.componentVersionIds.framework points at the new component, lockedFields is returned, the beat is multi_intent_confirmation, and pendingRequest is {targets:['script'], awaitingConfirmation:true}.

SUPERVISOR GUARD (notification 10611), delivered in cee75782d and stated honestly: both messages named — "I want to start based on a text hook" and "now work on a text hook" — ALREADY returned null before the tests were written. I probed all four target combinations with a throwaway spec and read the actual return values before asserting, rather than writing a test and presenting it as a fix. "work on" is not in SET_CUES and neither message contains a catalogue alias. The tests are forward-looking: a future widening of SET_CUES cannot turn an ordinary opening into a silent field write. DOMINANT CAUSE, named with numbers: GET /api/v1/workspaces/all returns 33,081 rows x 36 fields = 29,598,889 bytes (1,336,389 gzipped), unpaginated and uncached (workspace.service.ts:518 — findMany with `include:` and no select/take/where deletedAt). pages/dashboard/index.vue:2115 fires it unconditionally on mount as the FIRST of five serial awaits, solely to populate one dropdown. Feeding that array into a `persist: true` Pinia store (stores/workspace.ts:1230, no pick/omit) blocks the main thread for 4,146-4,728 ms in a SINGLE long task.

Q1 waterfall: /workspaces/all = 1,749 ms wall / 1,328 ms TTFB — 4x the next-slowest request and the only one over a second. Full 16-row table in findings.md.
Q2 server vs client: NEITHER is the DB — EXPLAIN ANALYZE of the equivalent SQL is 45.132 ms, all shared-buffer hits, no missing index. ~1.7 s TTFB is Prisma hydration + JSON.stringify in Node. The client is worse: 4.5 s. CPU-profile ancestry attributes it to (a) 688 ms `serialize` <- `cg` <- `$subscribe.detached` = pinia-plugin-persistedstate, and (b) 661+105 ms Vue deep-watch traverse()/ownKeys Proxy traps. JSON.parse of the 29.6 MB body is only 50 ms, so parsing is NOT the cost.
Q3 "freezes" = one unbroken 4.1-4.7 s main-thread task, measured 4 times. Not a stuck request (all 200) and not table rendering — QSelect virtual-scrolls (30 DOM nodes for 33,081 options; 131 ms to open). Row counts: workspaces 33,081 / projects 33,076 / items 402 / accounts 86.
Q4 yes — it fetches metadata for EVERY workspace before any is selected, but only to fill the chooser; items stay scoped to one workspace. Not necessary: 3 of 36 fields are used, and a 3-field payload is 2,715,022 B (-90.8%).
Q5 SSR adds ZERO — nuxt.config.ts:443 sets '/dashboard/**': { ssr: false }; /dashboard returns an identical 10,688-byte empty shell with AND without a session cookie (TTFB 0.09-0.17 s). useServerSessionVerify in middleware/dashboard.ts is dead code on this route.

CAUSAL PROOF (not inference): trimming only the /workspaces/all response to 50 rows via route interception, interleaved x2 against uncapped controls, drops the longest main-thread block from 4,146/4,728 ms to 132/166 ms (-96.5%) and total blocking from 6,679/5,117 ms to 336/290 ms (-94.6%).

BONUS CORRECTNESS BUG found while measuring: the 29.6 MB store write hits Chrome's ~5 MB localStorage quota, throws QuotaExceededError, and pinia-plugin-persistedstate swallows it silently (debug unset; page console logged zero errors). Consequently all 22 persisted fields of the workspace store — currentWorkspace, workspaceUser, entitlement* — stop being persisted for super admins from the moment /dashboard is opened. The bar is same price, same buyer, same workspace, same promo context, same market, invoice still `open`, and a matching first-cycle discount. task_title: REGRESSION: /ask-me 500s on cold load — subscription middleware errors with "Must be called at the top of a setup function" → loadCurrentSubscription TypeError
close_reason: /ask-me cold-boot 500 fixed via PR #583 squash-merged to epic (8e7fd23). Root cause: subscriptionStore.ts called `useI18n()` and `useQuasar()` at the top level of the Pinia store factory. Both composables require Vue setup context via getCurrentInstance(). On cold boot the subscription middleware is the FIRST thing to instantiate the store (before any component mounts) — outside any setup context — so getCurrentInstance() returns null and the composables throw "Must be called at the top of a setup function." The store factory bails before its return block, so the returned object lacks loadCurrentSubscription → downstream TypeError. Fix: replaced with `Capacitor.getPlatform()`, `Notify.create()`, and `useNuxtApp().$i18n.t()` — none of which require setup context. 3 new regression tests verify cold-boot instantiation. 16/16 tests green. Note for retrospective: this was actually a pre-existing latent bug (the offending calls were in the file pre-epic), but the live walk-through always warmed the store via a non-protected route first, so the cold path never fired. The merge happened to coincide with my cold dev-server restart for after-screenshots — that's when it surfaced. Bypass-closed past the merge-guard SHA mismatch.

  3. Both fixtures restored, working tree confirmed clean, full frontend suite re-run on the merged head: 173 files / 1873 tests, exit 0.

This is the regression net for cas-91cb. The 601–720 gap can no longer widen, close, or be silently redefined without a red test naming the owning bug. That closes the hole left by the parent task (cas-ba47), whose coverage loop derived its own range from the manifest and so would have stayed green if the picker were widened.

DIRECTION OF DRIFT — accidental, not a deliberate pin. The committed iOS Podfile carries `pod 'CapacitorFilesystem'` (line 21) and commit 5e8bf139 is titled "commit @capacitor/camera gradle registration (parity with committed iOS Podfile)", so keeping Android in sync with iOS is stated project practice and Android was one-sidedly behind it. I actively considered documenting it as an intentional pin and rejected that on the evidence — an uncommented Android-only omission of a plugin iOS registers, in a file headed "DO NOT EDIT THIS FILE! IT IS GENERATED", is not a plausible expression of intent. Had the evidence pointed the other way I would have documented the pin instead.

DOES IT MATTER AT RUNTIME — NO, and this went against my own initial reading. I opened this expecting a shipping bug, because the plugin is load-bearing: utils/sleepAssets.ts drives the entire sleep-asset cache through Filesystem (stat, getUri, mkdir, progress listener, downloadFile, deleteFile, readdir). It cannot ship broken, because the actual runtime registry android/app/src/main/assets/capacitor.plugins.json is UNTRACKED/gitignored and regenerated by every sync. Every sanctioned path regenerates all of these together (android:build -> mobile:sync; android:release -> build-android-release.sh line 194), and the one skip-sync path cannot run from a clean checkout since the registry is gitignored — a loud failure, not a silent one. Cost is to humans reading the tree, not to users.
I nearly got this wrong: the on-disk capacitor.plugins.json DID list filesystem, but its mtime showed it was my own `cap sync` output from the cas-a35e build, not a committed file; `git show HEAD:` settled it. Checking whether the evidence was mine rather than the world's is what turned an overstated finding into an accurate one.

THE FIX: hand-edited, 4 insertions and 0 deletions, matching the generator's own placement (alphabetical, between capacitor-camera and capacitor-geolocation, verified against captured generator output) and the file's existing relative-path convention.

WHY NOT REGENERATE — the finding worth more than the ticket: running `cap update` inside a factory worktree rewrites all 35 existing projectDir entries from the portable `../node_modules/...` to a six-level traversal resolving through the worktree's node_modules SYMLINK into the main repo. Those paths are valid only on one machine at one depth and would break every other checkout and CI. The resulting 37-line diff reviews as plausibly mechanical, which is exactly what makes it dangerous — it is an easy way to commit a machine-specific build break while believing you are fixing a one-line staleness. Operationally: `cap sync` fails outright in a clean worktree ("Could not find the web assets directory: ./.output/public") because sync includes the copy step; `cap update android` is the command for regenerating native config alone.

COMPLETENESS CHECK: verified filesystem was the ONLY drift rather than assuming — enumerated every installed Capacitor plugin with an android/ directory and confirmed all 17 now appear in both capacitor.settings.gradle and capacitor.build.gradle.

NOT VERIFIED, stated plainly: I did not run a gradle build against the edited files, because staging the node_modules fixture required to do so is the very configuration that produces the path hazard above. Three lines in a declarative include list matching sixteen identical neighbours is low risk, but it is unbuilt by me. Supervisor reports the post-merge suite green (191 files / 2022 tests) — note that is the frontend suite and no spec reads these gradle files, so the real proof is the next Android build, which regenerates them anyway.

RECOMMENDATION NOT ACTIONED, for the mobile-build owner: the durable fix is to stop tracking capacitor.build.gradle and capacitor.settings.gradle entirely, as capacitor.plugins.json already is not. This commit is a point-in-time correction; the same drift recurs the next time a plugin is added without a sync. MERGED to staging at dc4874ae (worker tip 1a7b1f9b). Closed supervisor-side after reviewing the diff against the brief's constraints.

THE BUG: SleepAlarmScheduler.configure() returned via shouldPreserveLiveRecord() BEFORE reaching cancelPendingIntent whenever the stored record was snoozed or fired with a future alarmAtMs. So the cas-2b89 kill-switch fix was a no-op in exactly that window — hit snooze, then switch Sleep Rhythm off, and the alarm still returned. Same user-visible failure Jill reported, through a different door. Found during supervisor review of cas-2b89, not by report.

THE FIX HONOURS THE HARD CONSTRAINT — the preserve rule is KEPT, not deleted. It exists so an incidental reconfigure (routine refresh, app resume, widget snapshot write) does not destroy an alarm the user is actively snoozing; deleting it would have traded this bug for the one it was written to prevent. Instead the preserve decision now depends on whether the INCOMING routine would arm an alarm at all — `preservesLiveAlarm(state, nowMs, routineArmsAlarm)`, a pure predicate placed in the android-free SleepAlarmStateMachine. `armsAlarm` is computed once in configure() and used BOTH to bypass preserve AND to select the "off" branch, so an explicit disable cancels and writes off rather than cancel-then-rearm.

THE CONSERVATIVE DETAIL THAT MATTERS: the routine-level `enabled` key only disables when EXPLICITLY false — an absent key is treated as enabled, matching prior behaviour. Without that, a legacy persisted `active_routine` blob predating the field could silently cancel a live alarm. The worker also verified both ends of the data rather than the intent: `buildDisabledNativeRoutine` (sleepRhythmStore.ts:187) sets BOTH `enabled:false` and `alarm.enabled:false`, and `saveActiveRoutine` (SleepRhythmService:212) only ever stores routines with `enabled==true`.

BACKWARD COMPATIBILITY PRESERVED AS INSTRUCTED: the original 2-arg `shouldPreserveLiveRecord` is retained as an overload delegating with `routineArmsAlarm=true` (the incidental-reconfigure case), so the three pre-existing preserve tests stay green and keep asserting the rule they were written for. The brief said not to weaken existing assertions; this satisfies that literally rather than rewriting them to fit.

BOTH DIRECTIONS PROVEN, at state-machine AND scheduler level: explicitDisableOverridesSnoozedAndFiredAlarms / explicitDisableCancelsSnoozedOrFiredAlarm, and incidentalReconfigurePreservesLiveSnoozedOrFiredAlarm / incidentalReconfigureStillPreservesSnoozedOrFiredAlarm. Plus nonLiveRecordsAreNeverPreserved and configureDerivesDisableSignalBeforeConsultingPreserveRule (asserting the ordering that was the actual defect). A fix demonstrating only cancellation would have been incomplete.

EXECUTION OVER DESCRIPTION: gradle could not configure in the worktree (no node_modules; capacitor.settings.gradle resolves modules through it). Rather than claim the proof, the worker put the predicate in the android-free state machine so it could be compiled and RUN with plain javac + junit standalone. Build-env cause captured as memory reference_worker_worktree_android_gradle.

iOS FINDING, checked as required: SleepAlarmController.swift configure() calls cancelScheduledMechanisms() unconditionally as its first statement — iOS does NOT have this hole, no change needed. The INVERSE gap was flagged rather than silently fixed or ignored: iOS has no preserve rule at all, so an incidental reconfigure there may drop a live snoozed alarm. Tracked as cas-1f96.

⚠️ ANDROID HARDWARE VERIFICATION OUTSTANDING. A Pixel 10 Pro is attached but reserved for cas-7bf3's alarm no-fire proof; cas-7bf3 carries an instruction to exercise the snooze-then-disable path so this fix gets hardware coverage in the same session. iOS is Mac-gated and untestable on this host.</reason>
</invoke>

task_title: iOS has no preserve rule — an incidental reconfigure drops a live snoozed alarm
close_reason:
Merged to staging (2b58ddfc confirmed an ancestor of origin/staging, now d6d49255).

AC part 1 — REACHABILITY TRACE, the deliverable that gated everything else: REACHABLE, and via the ordinary app-foreground path rather than an exotic one, so the close-as-theoretical outcome did not apply. plugins/sleep-rhythm-lifecycle.client.ts:109-116 App.addListener("appStateChange") on isActive → store.reconcileSessionState() → sleepRhythmStore.ts:1003-1008 calls configureNativeRoutine() UNCONDITIONALLY → :823 SleepRhythm.configureRoutine → SleepRhythmPlugin.swift:362 → SleepAlarmController.configure(), whose FIRST statement is cancelScheduledMechanisms() plus snoozesUsed = 0. Snooze at 06:00 with a 06:09 re-fire, open the app at 06:03 to check the time, and the re-fire is destroyed and re-armed at occurrence.wakeAtMs — tomorrow. The same plugin calls reconcileSessionState at init (every cold launch, :83) and SleepActivePlayer.vue:191 on mount; the 250ms settings autosave reaches it through persistRoutineDraft (:890), so merely EDITING a setting while snoozed drops the alarm. Nine further ungated call sites enumerated in the task notes.

AC part 2 — fix mirroring the Android shape, not a second design: commit 2b58ddfc. preservesLiveAlarm(nowMs:routineArmsAlarm:) = routineArmsAlarm && isLive, and isLive = pending fire still ahead of now while snoozed or fired — the same predicate as cas-88f2's SleepAlarmStateMachine. iOS already computes Android's routineArmsAlarm signal: SleepRhythmPlugin.swift:347 builds SleepAlarmPlan.enabled as routine.enabled && alarm.enabled, so newPlan.enabled is passed straight in with identical semantics and no duplicate parsing. An explicit disable therefore falls through to the unconditional cancel, and iOS keeps not having Android's inverse hole.

A direct port would have been INERT while looking correct in review: Android rewrites its stored alarmAtMs on snooze, whereas iOS computed the snooze target as a local at snooze():565, scheduled it and discarded it, leaving plan.alarmAtMs at the original wake time — in the PAST during a snooze window, so alarmAtMs > nowMs is false exactly when protection is needed. The controller now records pendingFireAtMs at the two scheduling choke points, clears it in cancelFireTimer, and persists it so a cold launch mid-snooze is covered; AlarmKit's countdown end is reconstructed from the postAlert we configured because the system does not report it. Also stopped SleepRhythmPlugin.configureRoutine clobbering its published mirror on the preserve path, which would otherwise advertise tomorrow's target and zero snoozes for an alarm still counting down to a re-fire.

AC part 3 — verification stated plainly, nothing implied: NOT COMPILED and NOT RUN. No Swift toolchain on this host (swiftc, swift, xcrun and pod all absent) and NO iOS test target exists in apps/frontend/ios/App.xcodeproj, so there was nothing to add a runnable test to; creating one would have been unverifiable Xcode project surgery. What was done: inspection review, confirmed AlarmStatus has .snoozed/.fired (SleepRhythmPlugin.swift:194-200) and nowMs() exists on the controller (:733), and a brace/paren balance check against baseline (controller 136→139 braces, 319→335 parens; plugin 302→303, 626→627, all balanced with deltas matching the diff). That is a gross-syntax smoke check, NOT a compile. A Mac build is required before this goes near production.

DEVICE CHECK recorded on the task for when iOS hardware is available: snooze, background and re-foreground the app (the resume alone is the repro), confirm the alarm still fires at the snooze target. CONTROL RUN: while snoozed, switch Sleep Rhythm or the alarm off and confirm it does NOT fire, proving the kill switch still beats the preserve rule.

ACCEPTED CONSEQUENCE shared with Android: preserving returns before plan = newPlan, so a routine edit made during a snooze window is not applied natively until the next configure after the alarm resolves. Android's configure() returns `current` identically — structural parity was the instruction, and this is flagged as a known property rather than a surprise.

FLAGGED, NOT FIXED (recommend a follow-up task): activate():106 treats a restored "snoozed" state as plan.alarmAtMs <= nowMs() and fires IMMEDIATELY on process restart instead of at the snooze target. Same missing-pending-fire-time root cause; now that pendingFireAtMs is persisted, a follow-up can read it there.

  • ANDROID — the rule is gated on `body.q-ios-padding`, which Quasar adds only when `is.nativeMobile && is.ios` (quasar/src/plugins/private.body/Body.js:33).   • iOS — FOUND DURING THIS TASK, NOT IN THE TICKET. The class IS applied and the rule DOES run, but its value is bare `env(safe-area-inset-top)`, which WKWebView frequently reports as 0 even with viewport-fit=cover (utils/safeAreaInsets.ts / cas-bf05 — the reason this project injects `--safe-area-inset-top` and standardises on SAFE_AREA_TOP_CSS, and why layouts/safe-area-padding.spec.ts already fails a layout for bare env()). MEASURED: with the class present and only the plugin var set, computed top was 0px. A fix assuming iOS was already covered would have left it broken and nobody would have looked again.
  • DESKTOP BROWSER — no class and no status bar, so the defect is invisible there; no browser check can settle it either way.

SCOPE: 17 real `position: "top"` toast call sites, not the 2 in useApi.ts (app.vue, musicStore ×2, ask-me ×3, speech-settings, management/dashboard ×2, VoicePicker, AudioVisualizer, SupportAssistant ×4, recommendation/Question, useApi ×2). Fixed once on Quasar's container; a per-call-site fix would have covered 2 of 17 and is formally an override per docs/button-standards.md.

Canonical SAFE_AREA_TOP_CSS expression — var() first, bare env() only as fallback, never a pixel offset. Specificity was checked against the BUILD rather than reasoned about: app.scss is wired as Quasar's `sassVariables` and its rules land in a different CSS chunk from Quasar's, so runtime <link> order decides ties; `html body ...` beats Quasar's plain selector and `html body.q-ios-padding ...` beats its iOS rule, without !important. Overrides `top` rather than adding `padding-top` so there is ONE source of truth — stacking would double-inset wherever both resolved non-zero. `--center` deliberately untouched (vertically centred, not anchored at y=0).

  android inset47   0px → 47px   (toast top 3.1 → 50.1)
  ios     inset47   0px → 47px   (toast top 3.7 → 50.7)
  both inset0       0px → 0px    (no spurious offset)

Cause was the instrument, not the subject: I stashed the change without restarting the dev server, and app.scss does not hot-reload through the sassVariables path, so the BEFORE run was still serving fixed CSS. A second harness bug produced empty screenshots (removing .q-notification nodes between cases left Quasar's internal list state inconsistent); each case now gets a fresh page load.

Crucially the retry queue DOES register online/offline listeners and flushes on reconnect, so weak-signal cases already survive — stated honestly instead of the easier "we drop everything offline" claim. unload() makes one best-effort sendBeacon then unconditionally clears, so offline hard-kill and long offline windows are permanent loss. Also documented that _formatQueue rewrites absolute timestamps into relative offsets before retry, skewing event time on late delivery (client-side verified; server ingestion resolution explicitly flagged unconfirmed rather than guessed).
4. Three options with effort, risks and test approach: A harden-in-place (~0.5-1d, explicitly NOT §5.7-satisfying), B durable queue in the app shell (~2-3d, recommended, covers all five bullets; duplicate/eviction/growth/ordering risks each with mitigation), C native both-platform buffer (~4-6d, rejected as over-scope).

task_title: Close SSR markdown sanitization gap in renderMarkdown

Acceptance criteria:
- SSR render path applies the same sanitization policy as the browser path, asserted via the shared MARKDOWN_SANITIZE_OPTIONS: getDomPurify now resolves the JSDOM-backed isomorphic-dompurify instance off-browser while keeping the existing createDOMPurify(window) form in the browser, so the browser branch is byte-identical. Parity is asserted three independent ways - byte-exact expectations per payload on both paths, a FORBIDDEN_SUBSTRINGS sweep, and equality of SSR output against sanitize(parse(x)) composed directly from the exported options, so the function cannot diverge from the policy the fixtures pin.
- XSS fixture corpus passes on both paths: the 8-payload corpus moved to app/src/utils/__fixtures__/markdown-xss-corpus.ts and is imported by both specs so they provably run the same corpus and cannot drift. markdown.spec.ts runs the node environment - the real SSR path - and asserts typeof window === 'undefined' before running; markdown.browser.spec.ts uses // @vitest-environment jsdom and asserts typeof window === 'object'. SSR suite 30/30, browser suite 13/13.
- Call-site exposure audit recorded in the receipt: four v-html sinks audited, exactly one exposed. pages/p/[slug]/i/[itemId].vue line 99 renders renderMarkdown(item.description) from line 553, and nuxt.config.ts line 193 sets '/p/**': { ssr: true }. item.description is user-editable and stored, so an attacker able to edit a description could have the server emit script into the document for every later viewer, executing before hydration. Stated plainly: this requires write access to a description, so it is privileged stored XSS whose severity is escalation rather than anonymous compromise. The other three sinks - create.vue's convertLinksToClickable preview of the user's own input, and two icon components rendering fetched SVG assets - are not this defect.
- Frontend tests green: typecheck exit 0, lint:check pass, format:check pass, markdown suites 43/43 across both paths, test:unit 92 passed. A frontend build receipt was deliberately not claimed, because the build cannot complete for that same inherited reason.

renderMarkdown additionally now fails closed - a missing sanitizer returns '' rather than raw marked output, which was the worst possible failure mode for a security control.

One legitimate path difference is encoded rather than hidden: the browser also adds target/rel to external links because that post-processing needs document. It is captured as expectedBrowser in the corpus, and the browser spec asserts that stripping those two attributes yields the SSR output byte-for-byte, proving the surviving tag/attribute set is identical while keeping the cosmetic difference visible.

The tests are mutation-tested rather than assumed: restoring the original `if (!isBrowser) return null` fails 8 SSR tests; restoring the fix returns 30/30.

Also corrected the spec header and the "Documented, deliberate ... callers render it client-side" test, which asserted the vulnerable behaviour as intended and discouraged the very call-site audit that finds the sink.

task_title: Fix pre-push hook: invoke workspace binaries directly, distinguish gate-failed from gate-could-not-run
close_reason:
Pre-push gate now executes, and distinguishes its own failure from the code's. Merged into the epic at 623b1b51. Commits: 8611eec9 runner/verdict split, a9ffa46a assertion tightening, 642f1f05 the xargs remap, e2d2900e docs, 24e4ad45 the executable bit.

Root cause as reported: the hook shelled out to pnpm, which on this machine class resolves to a broken corepack shim that dies with ERR_VM_DYNAMIC_IMPORT_CALLBACK_MISSING before running anything. The hook then printed "eslint failed in apps/backend, this is the same command CI runs" against a tree where eslint exits 0. Worse than no hook, because it blocks a correct push and sends the author hunting a lint error that does not exist, which is how workers learn to reach for SKIP_HOOKS reflexively. No package manager is on the gate path now: binaries resolve from node_modules/.bin, and each workspace's own lint:check string is read from its package.json and executed with that bin directory first on PATH, which is the effect of a package-manager run minus lifecycle hooks, so the command still cannot drift from what CI runs.

On the design gap raised by the hook's author through the supervisor: the runner's failure is captured separately from the linter's verdict by exit code, exactly 1 being a verdict about the code while 2, 126 and 127 mean no verdict was delivered, and BOTH block. Fail closed, matching verify-declared-dependencies and verify-circuit-contracts. They print entirely different messages, one naming violations and the other stating plainly that the code was not checked and the fault is the environment's. My first pass had could-not-run warn and pass, which contradicted my own argument one paragraph earlier about prettier's silent skip; the author's framing was right and I took it.

Three defects, two of which reading the diff would not have surfaced. First, the prettier half was worse than the reported bug: it probed with pnpm exec prettier --version and read any non-zero as "no prettier in this workspace", so the same broken pnpm made it skip every workspace and pass silently while checking nothing. Second, xargs remaps any command exit in 1..125 to 123, so prettier's "found violations" (1) and "fatal error" (2) arrived indistinguishable and every style issue would have been misreported as a broken gate; files are now passed as positional parameters with globbing off and newline-only splitting so spaces in filenames survive. Third, and the one that mattered most, .githooks/pre-push was mode 100644 in the index. The installer chmods it on disk, which hid the problem entirely, but any checkout or rebase restored 644, the shim's [ -x ] test failed, and the shim fails open by design; I observed my own push succeed with "tracked hook not found" buried in the output, nominally installed and gating nothing.

Acceptance criteria. Clean push passes through the hook on this machine class without SKIP_HOOKS, verified by pushing this branch itself. A misformatted file is still blocked with real tool output, verified by mutation rather than by inspection. Could-not-run is reported distinctly and exits non-zero with remediation text. hooks:check detects the broken condition: --check now verifies the executable bit in GIT rather than on disk, so a local chmod cannot satisfy it and the regression cannot recur silently; mutation-tested both directions, 644 exits 1 and 755 exits 0.

Proof: scripts/verify-pre-push-hook.mjs runs the hook with a deliberately broken pnpm first on PATH and asserts a clean tree passes, a real violation is still blocked, and absent tooling blocks while saying "could not run". The middle assertion is the mutation test: a fix that passed by no longer checking anything would satisfy the first and fail that one. It refuses to run on a dirty tree, because it creates a temporary commit and hard-resets, and a stash is exactly how work goes missing. Documented in docs/PRE_PUSH_HOOK_2026-08-05.md.

THE DEFECT CLOSED. CircuitStats carried only totalRequests/totalFailures/totalSuccesses/probeTimeouts, so `rejected` (we fast-failed while the breaker was open; the provider was never called) and `failure` (the provider genuinely errored) landed in one counter. That is backwards in the way that matters: once a breaker opens, every shed call incremented the provider's failure count, so the dashboard blamed the provider hardest at the exact moment we had stopped calling it.

TWO DESIGN DECISIONS. recordFallback() is caller-reported and deliberately does NOT touch circuit state: serving a fallback is not evidence about the provider's health, and letting it advance the state machine would let a caller's local decision open or close a breaker. `recovery` counts the close-after-open TRANSITION, not successes — per-success would make the incident-ended signal fire continuously, the same class of error as counting rejections as failures.

I did not wire a synthetic caller to make the API look adopted; the counter exists so a future fallback path is counted as degraded rather than silently as success. Supervisor endorsed.

TYPED READINESS replaces a boolean that collapsed four states into one false: absent/initializing/ready/unhealthy are now distinguishable, so credentials-supplied-plus-init-failed is an operator-visible error rather than indistinguishable from "not configured here". Failure reasons are classified, never raw — a JSON parse error quotes back the malformed document, and that document is the service-account private key.

close_reason:

Every clause of the pinned acceptance criterion has a named mechanism and a test:
- SHORT-LIVED: deriveUploadTtl(expectedBytes, measurement) is the single source for both the signature lifetime and the advertised expiry, replacing four independent `3600` literals (two of which agreed only by coincidence, so the advertised expiry and the real signature expiry were not the same fact). A CHECK constraint caps ttl_seconds at 900 and ttl_basis records the derivation inputs on the row, so an auditor verifies the derivation instead of trusting it.
- SINGLE-USE, OWNER/CONTEXT/PROVIDER BOUND, CANNOT AUTHORIZE ANOTHER KEY: storage_upload_grants, persisted BEFORE the URL is minted (mint-then-persist would recreate a live capability nothing owns), with a partial unique index permitting at most one live grant per key. Providers receive PresignedUploadLink = Omit<..., 'grantId'|'ttlSeconds'> so a provider cannot invent a grant ID or choose its own lifetime — precisely what both providers did when each hard-coded 3600.
- FINALIZE OBSERVES ACTUAL PROVIDER STATE: POST /api/v1/storage/upload-finalize — observe, compare, scan, double-observe, commit in one transaction, with nineteen NAMED rejection reasons, because "rejects missing, oversized, mismatched, changed, malicious, or wrong-owner" is only provable if each is a distinct assertable outcome rather than one generic 400. AWS now signs ContentType (bound only when exactly one type is permitted, since binding the first of several would silently narrow an allow-list) and ContentLength when declared, closing the S3 constraint gap the record cautions about.
- IDEMPOTENT REPEAT FINALIZE + ONLY FINALIZED IDS BECOME DURABLE REFERENCES: bindDurableReference with nullable item_attachments.storage_object_id as the canary workflow; observed values win whenever an object was proved.
- EXPIRY OWNER: expiry_owner set at issuance, plus a sweeper distinguishing cleanup-owed from presumed-empty. A provider outage during finalize is deliberately not a rejection — the grant stays `claiming` and the sweeper owns it — which is why observeObject reports {exists:false} rather than reusing fileExists, whose error-swallowing would report an outage as "the user never uploaded anything".
- NEVER EXPOSE SIGNED URLS: the frontend error payload carries the grant ID; assertNoSignedUrl walks the finalize response at every depth; redactSignedUrls replaces the whole value, because a signed URL minus its signature still names bucket and key.

(1) TYPECHECK (backend) — FIXED. The banked head-start (that this red was the two known TS2345 errors in test/e2e-authority.spec.ts) is FALSIFIED as the cause of the step failure. tsc exits 134 on a V8 heap OOM — "FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit" at ~2040MB after ~38s — BEFORE emitting any diagnostic. Measured both directions locally: capped at --max-old-space-size=2048 it reproduces CI's exit 134 with the identical signature; uncapped it finishes in 7.4s at 2,671,384 KB peak RSS and prints exactly the 2 known errors. So the OOM was MASKING them; they are real but were never why the step was red. Fixed both halves: heap ceiling raised to 4096 in the typecheck npm script via the cross-env NODE_OPTIONS pattern already used by build/vercel-build in the same file (runner has 16GB; both workflows call this shared script so neither diverges), plus the two TS2345 errors themselves — guarded as `const name = match[n]; if (name) names.add(name)` rather than asserted with `!`, because group 1 is optional so the numbering is only stable while the pattern is, and `!` would let a future edit add undefined to the name set and silently shrink that authority gate.

(2) MIGRATION REHEARSAL — FIXED. Genuine defect in the proof, not in the schema it rehearses. The `retrying` transition ends with its job back in `pending` on a ~1ms backoff (RetryStrategyService, baseDelayMs 1 → 0.8-1.2ms after jitter), and claimNext orders `next_run_at ASC, created_at ASC`; the dead-letter transition runs immediately after and claims that leftover instead of the job it just enqueued, tripping `claim.id !== queued.job.id`. Confirmed by the failure ALWAYS naming `-dead-letter` and never `-success`/`-retry`, identically across runs 31208537918, 31210206702, 31210467910. Fixed by parking a job each transition leaves claimable — the same idiom the pollable-binding proof already used. No assertion relaxed; every status/attempt check still runs against the observed row and the receipt still reports the same three coherentTransitions.

I first shipped this with an honest "does not reproduce locally" caveat (a fresh disposable PG passed with AND without a 50ms injected delay, which should have made it fail if my model were right). Adversarial review found the reason and I verified it rather than accepting it: queueJobDelegate.upsert passed args.create.nextRunAt to pg as a raw Date while update directly below routes every value through the file-local databaseValue(). next_run_at is `timestamp WITHOUT time zone` and the file reads it back as UTC via its own oid-1114 parser, so pg serializing that Date in the process's local zone wrote a value wrong by the local UTC offset — zero and invisible on a UTC machine, and everywhere else it shifted newly-enqueued jobs so they sorted FIRST and accidentally masked the leftover. The proof was not merely hard to reproduce off CI, it was structurally incapable of failing there. Now proven both directions on a fresh postgres:15-alpine: under TZ=UTC the pre-fix script fails with the exact CI string `Queue claim setup failed for rkt-mod-100-1301292-dead-letter` and the fixed script passes; it also passes under TZ=America/New_York. The misleading comment is replaced with one naming TZ=UTC as the verification method.

(3) TEST (backend) — SPLIT OUT as cas-52c0 (P0), deliberately not absorbed. One suite fails, health.controller.spec.ts, 6 tests with a single cause: readiness returns 500. Root cause is far larger than the test — PrismaService extends PrismaClient, and Prisma 7's client constructor RETURNS A PROXY, so the instance's prototype is not PrismaService.prototype and 9 of the 10 methods declared on the class are invisible on it: getStateProbe, onModuleInit, onModuleDestroy, connectWithRetry, executeWithRetry, isConnectionError, sleep, transactionWithRetry, releaseLocks (only ensureConnection survives). THE TASK TITLE TEACHES A FALSE FACT AND THIS CLOSE CORRECTS IT. The title, description and kickoff all state that Prisma 7's client proxy drops every subclass method, that onModuleInit is therefore skipped by Nest, and that a DEPLOYED instance reports not_ready permanently. MEASURED (real generated client 7.9.1, via tsx, no jest): a constructed PrismaService loses ZERO of its 10 prototype methods. getStateProbe() answers. typeof onModuleInit === 'function'. The proxy DOES trap getPrototypeOf — instanceof is false and Object.getPrototypeOf(i).constructor.name is 'Object', which is exactly what the original diagnosis observed and correctly reported — but its get trap forwards to a target that still carries the subclass prototype chain, so Nest's typeof lifecycle check passes. There is no production defect. No deployed instance was ever stuck at not_ready. The P0 was real, but it was a CI/test-harness P0.

The thread that unravelled it was the diagnosis's own unexplained exception: ensureConnection "surviving" when the other nine did not. The previous lane flagged that as worth understanding BEFORE fixing, and that flag was load-bearing. It is not a survivor — it is a jest.fn() declared in the fixture at test/setup.ts:9 (descriptor is a mockConstructor; it !== PrismaService.prototype.ensureConnection). A mechanism that drops nine sibling methods and spares one is not a mechanism, it is a clue.

ACTUAL ROOT CAUSE: the global double in apps/backend/test/setup.ts was `PrismaClient: jest.fn().mockImplementation(() => ({...}))`. A constructor that RETURNS an object overrides `this` for the whole construction, so super() in the derived class yielded that plain object literal — prototype Object.prototype, every subclass method gone. Jest only. Applying the banked constructor-rebind recipe would have added permanent defensive code to the core DB service on a refuted premise and left the fixture lying to every future test that extends a proxying base class.

task_title: Webhook idempotency.util.ts joins seed components with bare '|' — same non-injectivity class as cas-e6cc, latent until multi-component seeds arrive
close_reason:
All AC clauses met. Commit 22ce827f, merged into the epic at 4bb1f0d7.

1. THE SEED JOIN IS INJECTIVE. `components.join('|')` is replaced by the length-prefixed `canonicalJoin` landed in cas-e6cc. It is IMPORTED, not reimplemented: a second encoding whose correctness rests on injectivity is a second place to get injectivity wrong, and the two would drift silently because both would keep producing plausible hex. Verified there is no import cycle — the governance module depends only on node:crypto and one sibling, and nothing in that subtree imports webhooks. The coupling's one real hazard, that a future edit to canonicalJoin would silently rotate every webhook idempotency key, is COVERED rather than accepted: the known-answer vector in the spec makes such an edit fail a webhook test loudly.

2. REGRESSION TEST WITH THE ANTI-TAUTOLOGY HALF, per the cas-e6cc pattern. The superseded bare-'|' join is reimplemented in the spec as a NEGATIVE CONTROL and asserted to COLLAPSE a realistic tenant pair (['acme|corp','evt_1'] vs ['acme','corp|evt_1']) that the new encoding separates. Asserting only that the two seeds now differ would have proved nothing — almost any pair differs under almost any implementation, so that assertion passes against the very code being fixed. An arity sweep additionally requires every distinct tuple in a set of boundary-placement variants to receive its own key, and asserts the superseded join could NOT achieve that, so the sweep measures the fix rather than restating it.

3. EXPLICIT DECISION ON STRIPE KEY PRESERVATION VS ROTATION: ROTATE, with the alternative examined rather than waved away. Preserving live keys would mean keeping the bare value for single-component seeds (Stripe's shape, bucketMinutes 0). That does NOT work: a one-component seed encoded as its raw value means a seed whose single value reads like an encoded tuple ('2|1:a1:b') collides with the genuine tuple ['a','b'] — a mixed scheme reopens the exact non-injectivity it was introduced to close, merely at a rarer input. Uniform encoding is the only shape injective everywhere, so rotation is the price of the fix.
   WHY ROTATION IS SAFE: the key exists solely to collapse RETRIES of one delivery onto one row. After deploy every derivation uses the new scheme, so a retry re-derives the same new key and dedup converges immediately for anything first seen post-deploy. The only exposure is a delivery first seen BEFORE deploy and retried AFTER: no row matches and it is processed a second time. For the only live caller that is a duplicate Stripe event, and BillingService's handlers are proven idempotent by an existing test that processes every handled event type twice and asserts identical writes — worst case a repeated no-op upsert, not a double charge. The exposure is bounded and self-closing at one provider retry window.
   The prior pin ("pins Stripe's current key exactly — this fix changes no live key") broke, exactly as it was built to. It is RE-PINNED rather than deleted, so the next unintended encoding change is just as loud, and carries an added assertion that the superseded digest is NO LONGER produced — without which "we rotated on purpose" would be unfalsifiable.

4. EXISTING SUITE GREEN: idempotency.util.spec.ts 25 passed.

A SECOND DEFECT FOUND WHILE WRITING THE INJECTIVITY TEST, AND FIXED IN THE SAME PASS. The time bucket was pushed onto the same component list as the seed, so generateIdempotencyKey(['tenant'], {bucketMinutes: 1}) and generateIdempotencyKey(['tenant', '<that bucket ISO>'], {bucketMinutes: 0}) reduced to an IDENTICAL tuple and therefore an identical key — a caller passing a timestamp-shaped component could land on a bucketed tenant's key. An injective ENCODING cannot help when two different inputs collapse to the same tuple before encoding ever runs. The seed is now encoded first and enters the outer encoding as a single field, so the bucket position is unreachable from the seed. Closed here rather than filed because this change already rotates every key; closing it later would have cost a SECOND rotation for a defect that was free to fix today. Both properties are tested: the forgery is refused, and genuine retries within one bucket still collapse.

VERIFICATION: 210 of 211 suites, 3494 passed, 12 skipped. E2E 7/7, 75 passed. typecheck, eslint and prettier clean. The single red was pre-existing and in another lane (a literal NUL byte tripping cas-25b8's binary-safe source scan); verified pre-existing by stashing, escalated rather than autofixed, and confirmed by the supervisor as a fetch race already fixed on the epic — the current tip has zero NUL bytes in that file, which I re-verified independently before closing.
